en: Preface by Śramaṇa Sengrui to the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, Scroll One.
The *Madhyamaka-śāstra* consists of five hundred verses, composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna. It takes the Middle Way as its...
A name illuminates its reality;
employing a discourse as its designation exhausts its expression.
Since reality is not realized without names, one relies upon them to proclaim it.
It is said that nothing can be fully exhausted through mere exegesis; therefore, I employ this treatise to elucidate it.

Once its reality has been proclaimed and its words have been clarified, the conduct of the Bodhisattva and the illumination of the site of enlightenment will be understood with vivid and spontaneous clarity.
Stagnant delusion arises from inverted views, by which one sinks and drowns within the three realms;
partial awakening arises from the intellect of aversion, by which one becomes obstinate and falls into discord.

Thus we know that great awakening resides in expansive illumination, while petty wisdom is entangled in a narrow mind. If illumination is not expansive, it is insufficient to level existence and non-existence or unify the mundane and the sacred; if knowledge is not exhaustive, one cannot yet traverse the middle way to obliterate the two boundaries. That the mundane and the sacred are not leveled and the two boundaries are not obliterated is the concern of the Bodhisattva.
Therefore, the Great Being Nāgārjuna analyzed [reality] through the Middle Way, causing those who follow the path of delusion to undergo a single transformation upon beholding his profound guidance;
he encompassed all through the principle of "immediate transformation," leading those guests of profound awakening to lose their need for inquiry upon attaining the dawn-like clarity of realization.

Vast and expansive indeed! It may truly be called the opening of a level path upon the profound steps and the unshuttering of the mysterious gate within the world; it fans the wind of wisdom through the withered branches and lets the nectar of ambrosia flow upon the parched and emaciated.

When the construction of a hundred-beamed palace is undertaken, one despises the humble thatch hut; when one beholds the grandeur and vastness of this discourse, one realizes the pettiness and perversity of partial enlightenment.
How fortunate it is for this region of the Central Realm (Zhōngguó) to suddenly have Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa moved here to serve as its guardian;
how the rugged and biased sentiments of the borderlands have come to receive the lingering grace of its radiant light.
From this time forward, those sages who discourse on the Way may finally be considered capable of discussing reality.

It is said that among the various kingdoms of India, there are none among the ranks of scholars who do not study and savor this treatise as their essential core; indeed, those who have taken up the brush to provide commentaries and explanations are quite numerous.

What is now being presented here is the commentary by the Indian Brahmin named Piṅgala—known as Qingmu (Blue Eye) in the language of Qin—who, although he possessed faith and understanding of the profound Dharma, was not elegant or refined in his phrasing.

Within this work, the Dharma Master has edited out all that was inconsistent, deficient, or redundant, and has fully elucidated the underlying principles of the sutra; yet, in some instances, the phrasing may still be slightly imperfect.

The *Śata-śāstra* governs the external to restrain heterodoxy, while this text (the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*) dispels internal stagnation; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is profound and vast, and the *Dvādaśamukha-samādhi-śāstra* is precise and penetrating. To seek these four works is truly like having the sun and moon enter one’s breast; there is nothing they do not illuminate with clear and thorough insight.

I have played with and savored it, unable to let go of my hands; thus, forgetting my own vulgarity and clumsiness, I entrust my enlightened sentiments to this preface, and have inscribed the titles and categories of its meanings at the head.
How could one have expected that it could be explained?
It is simply the joy of feeling one's own affinity with it.
Neither arising nor ceasing, neither permanent nor annihilated.
Neither identical nor different, neither coming nor departing;
He who can explain these dependent origination conditions, Who skillfully extinguishes all conceptual proliferation—
To that Buddha, the foremost among all teachers, I prostrate in reverence.
Question:
For what reason was this treatise composed? Answer:

Some say that all things arise from Maheśvara; some say they arise from Viṣṇu; some say they arise from the conjunction [of causes]; some say they arise from time; some say they arise from primordial nature (prakṛti); some say they arise from transformation; some say they arise spontaneously; and some say they arise from atoms.

Because of such errors as these, they fall into wrong views such as those of no cause, false causes, nihilism, and eternalism; they variously propound a self and what belongs to a self, and do not understand the True Dharma.

Desiring to sever such various false views and cause them to know the Buddha-dharma, the Buddha first taught the twelve links of dependent origination within the Śrāvaka teachings. Furthermore, for those who have already practiced and possess the great resolve capable of receiving the profound Dharma, he taught the characteristics of dependent origination through the Mahāyāna, namely that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, neither identical nor different, and are ultimately empty and non-existent.
As it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
The Buddha told Subhūti,
"When a bodhisattva sits at the site of enlightenment, he contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination as being like space, inexhaustible."

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the five hundred years of the Semblance Dharma, the faculties of sentient beings will become increasingly dull and they will become deeply attached to all phenomena. Seeking the definitive characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and so forth, they will fail to understand the Buddha’s true intent and instead cling merely to the literal words. When they hear it said in the Mahāyāna teachings that all things are ultimately empty, they will not know by what causes and conditions things are empty, and will immediately give rise to views of doubt.
"If all things are ultimately empty, how can one differentiate between sin and merit, or their retributions?
If this were so, there would be neither the conventional truth nor the ultimate truth."
"Taking up these marks of emptiness and giving rise to craving and attachment, they produce various errors regarding ultimate emptiness.
For the sake of such individuals, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna composed this *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*."
“Neither arising nor ceasing, neither permanent nor annihilated,
neither identical nor different, neither coming nor going.
One who can thus explain dependent origination skillfully extinguishes all conceptual proliferation.”
"I prostrate in worship to the Buddha, the foremost among all teachers.
By praising the Buddha with these two verses, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) has already been briefly explained.
Question:
Since all phenomena (*dharma*) are immeasurable, why are they refuted by means of only these eight matters? Answer:
Although dharmas are immeasurable, to briefly explain them through eight points constitutes a comprehensive refutation of all dharmas.

Regarding "non-arising," various masters have offered diverse explanations of the characteristic of arising: some claim that cause and effect are identical; others claim they are different; some claim the effect pre-exists within the cause, while others claim it does not; some claim there is arising from self-nature, some from another, and some from both; and some claim there is arising, while others claim there is no arising.
Such explanations regarding the characteristic of arising are all untenable; this matter shall be explained in detail later.
Since the characteristic of arising is definitively unobtainable, there is no arising.
As for non-extinction: if there is no arising, how could there be extinction?
Because there is neither arising nor ceasing, the remaining six matters are likewise non-existent.
Question: By means of "non-arising" and "non-ceasing," all phenomena have already been refuted in their entirety.
Why are six matters further explained?
The answer is:
it is for the purpose of establishing the meaning of neither arising nor ceasing.
There are those who do not accept non-arising and non-ceasing, yet believe in neither permanence nor annihilation.
If one seeks deeply into this lack of permanence and annihilation, it is itself non-arising and non-ceasing.

Why is this? If dharmas truly existed, they should not become non-existent; for that which previously existed and now does not is termed "annihilation. If there were a prior inherent nature, it would be "eternal. Therefore, by teaching neither eternal nor annihilated, one enters the meaning of neither arising nor ceasing.
Some may claim that although they have heard the fourfold refutation of all dharmas, they nonetheless establish all dharmas through four gates;
this too is not so.

If [the cause and effect] were identical, there would be no conditions; if they were different, there would be no continuity. This will be refuted in various ways later; therefore, it is further stated that they are neither identical nor different.
There are some who, although they have heard that the six causes refute all dharmas, still maintain that all dharmas arise and are established through "coming" and "going.
Those who speak of "coming" say that all dharmas come from such sources as Maheśvara, Prakṛti, or atoms; those who speak of "going" say that they return and go back to their original place.
Furthermore, all things are without arising.
Why? Because they are perceived by the world.
The eyes of the world see that grain was not produced at the beginning of the kalpa. Why is this?
Because apart from the grain of the beginning of the kalpa, the grain of today cannot be found.
If there were present-day grain apart from the grain at the beginning of the kalpa, then it would have to arise;
however, this is not actually the case, and for this reason it does not arise.
Question:
If it does not arise, then it should cease.
He replied:
"It does not cease."
Why is this? Because it is directly perceived by the world.
With their own eyes, people of the world see that grain from the beginning of the eon has not perished.
If it were destroyed, there should not be grain now;
yet grain actually exists, therefore it is not destroyed.
Question:
If it were not extinguished, it would have to be permanent.
He replied:
It is not permanent.
Why is this? Because it is directly perceived by the world.
The eyes of the world see that all things are impermanent; for example, when a grain sprouts, the seed then undergoes transformation and destruction. Therefore, they are not permanent.
Question: If it were not eternal, it would have to be subject to cessation. Answer:
It is not interrupted. Why?
Because it is directly perceived in the world.
The worldly eye perceives that all things are not severed; for example, as a sprout arises from a grain, they are therefore not severed.
If they were severed, there would be no continuity. Question:
If that were so, then all things would be one.
He replied:
"They are not one."
Why is this? Because it is directly perceived by the world.
The eyes of the world see that the myriad things are not identical; for example, a grain does not become a sprout, and a sprout does not become a grain.
If the grain were to become the sprout and the sprout were to become the grain, they would have to be one;
however, in reality this is not so, and therefore they are not one.
Question:
If they were not identical, they would have to be different.
He replied:
"They are not different."
Why is this? Because it is directly perceived by the world.
With their eyes, people in the world see that all things are not different.

If they were different, why would one distinguish between the grain sprout, the grain stem, and the grain leaf, rather than speaking of the tree sprout, the tree stem, and the tree leaf? Therefore, they are not different.
Question:
If they are not different, there ought to be coming. Answer:
There is no coming.
Why? Because it is directly perceived by the world.
The worldly eye perceives that all things do not come; for example, the sprout within a grain of rice comes from nowhere.
If it were to come, the sprout would have to arrive from another location, like a bird coming to perch upon a tree;
yet this is not the case, and therefore there is no coming.
Question:
If there is no coming, there should be an exit. Answer:
It does not emerge.
Why? Because it is directly perceived in the world.
The worldly eye sees that all things do not emerge.
If they were to emerge, one should see the sprout emerge from the grain, just as a snake emerges from its hole;
yet in reality this is not so, and therefore there is no emergence.
Question: Although you have explained the meaning of non-arising and non-ceasing, I wish to hear what the author of the treatise has said. Answer:
"Phenomena do not arise from themselves, Nor do they arise from another, Neither from both together nor without cause;
Therefore, know them to be unarisen. Regarding "not arising from themselves":
among the myriad things, none arise from their own essence; they necessarily depend upon various causes.
Furthermore, if [an entity] were produced from its own self-nature, then a single dharma would possess two natures:
first, the act of production; second, that which produces.
If it were produced from its own self-nature independently of other causes, then there would be neither cause nor condition.
Furthermore, if birth were to give rise to further birth, then birth would be infinite.
Since self does not exist, other also does not exist. Why is this so?
Because there is a self, there is an other.
If it does not arise from itself, nor does it arise from another, then arising from both would entail two faults:
namely, the faults of arising from self and arising from another.
If all things existed without a cause, they would be eternal; however, this is not the case.
Without a cause, there can be no effect.

If effects could exist without a cause, then those who practice generosity and observe the precepts would fall into hell, while those who commit the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes would be reborn in heaven, simply because there would be no cause.
Furthermore:
"Just as the intrinsic nature of all phenomena does not exist within conditions,
because they lack intrinsic nature, extrinsic nature likewise does not exist."
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena does not reside within the various conditions; it is only through the conjunction of these conditions that names are obtained.
Intrinsic nature is the very essence itself, and this essence is absent within the conditions.
Because intrinsic nature does not exist, there is no arising from self; because intrinsic nature does not exist, extrinsic nature also does not exist.
Why is this? It is because extrinsic nature exists in dependence upon intrinsic nature, and for that which is other, it is also its own intrinsic nature.
If self-nature is refuted, then other-nature is also refuted; therefore, it should not arise from other-nature.
If both self-nature and other-nature are refuted, then the meaning of "both" is also refuted.
To have no cause entails a great error; even that which has a cause can still be refuted, how much more so that which has no cause!
Since it cannot be found arising within the four propositions, it is therefore unarisen.
Question: The Abhidharmikas say that "all dharmas arise from four conditions. Why do you say they do not arise?
What are the four conditions?

"Conditions by way of cause, conditions by way of immediate succession, Conditions by way of object, and conditions by way of dominance— These four conditions give rise to all phenomena; There is no fifth condition.
All possible conditions are subsumed within these four; it is through these four conditions that all things come into being.
The causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
The sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*) excludes the final mind and mental factors of an Arhat in the past and present; it consists of all other past and present minds and mental factors.
The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) comprise all phenomena.
The answer is:
"Does the fruit arise from conditions, or does it arise from non-conditions?
Do these conditions possess a fruit, or do these conditions lack a fruit?"
If one asserts that there is a fruit, does this fruit arise from conditions or does it arise from non-conditions?
If one asserts that there are conditions, do these conditions possess a fruit or are they without a fruit?
Both [positions] are incorrect. Why?
"That dharma from which a fruit arises is called a condition."
"If the fruit has not yet arisen, why is it not called 'non-condition'?
Conditions have no fixed nature. Why is this so?
If the fruit has not yet arisen, at that time it cannot be called a condition;
it is only because we see the fruit arising from conditions that they are designated as "conditions.
The establishment of the condition depends upon the fruit, for the fruit comes later while the condition precedes it.
If the fruit does not yet exist, how can it be called a condition?

For example, because the combination of earth, water, and so forth gives rise to a jar, one perceives the jar as the condition and thereby knows that earth, water, and the rest are the conditions for the jar.
If the jar has not yet arisen, why are water, earth, and so forth not called "non-conditions"?
Therefore, the effect does not arise from conditions.
Since even conditions do not produce it, how much less so non-conditions?
Furthermore:
"If the effect were already present within the conditions, it would be neither existent nor non-existent.
If it were previously non-existent, for what would they be conditions? If it were already existent, what use would there be for conditions?"
Within the conditions, there is neither a pre-existing fruit nor an absent fruit.
If the fruit already existed beforehand, they could not be called "conditions," because the fruit would have already been present.
If the fruit did not exist beforehand, they likewise could not be called "conditions," because they would not produce anything else.
Question:
You have already refuted all causes and conditions in general; now I wish to hear the refutation of each individual condition. Answer:
"If a fruit does not arise from existence, nor does it arise from non-existence,
nor does it arise from both existence and non-existence, how can one say that there are conditions?
If conditions were able to produce a fruit, there would have to be three possibilities:
Whether it be existent, non-existent, or both existent and non-existent—
as stated in the preceding verse— if the effect already exists within the conditions, one should not say that it "arises," because it already exists.

If the fruit did not exist previously, one should not say that it arises, because it would not have existed beforehand; furthermore, it would be identical to that which is not a condition (*pratyaya*).
As for the claim that neither existence nor non-existence arises: "existence and non-existence" refers to being half-existent and half-non-existent, and both positions entail logical faults.
Furthermore, existence is contrary to non-existence, and non-existence is contrary to existence; how can a single dharma possess two such characteristics?
Since the characteristic of the arising of a fruit cannot be found when sought in these three ways, how can one say that there are causes and conditions?
Regarding the condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*):
"If the fruit has not yet arisen, then there should be no cessation;
how could a dharma that has ceased serve as a condition?"
"Therefore, there is no condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
All mental states and mental concomitants (*citta-caitta*) arise in succession throughout the three periods of time.
When the present mental states and mental concomitants cease, they act as the immediate antecedent condition for the future mind.
Future dharmas have not yet arisen; with what, then, could they act as a sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
If future dharmas already existed, they would already be "arisen," so what need would there be for a sequential condition?

Present moments of mind and mental factors have no time of abiding; if they do not abide, how can they serve as a sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)? If they were to abide, they would not be conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Why is this? Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) always possess the characteristic of cessation (*nirodhalakṣaṇa*).
Once they have ceased, they cannot serve as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
If one were to say that a ceased phenomenon still exists, it would follow that it is eternal (*nitya*); if it were eternal, there would be no such things as demerit or merit (*apuṇya-puṇya*).

If it is claimed that at the time of cessation it can act as a sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), then at the time of cessation it would be half-ceased and half-unceased; yet there is no third dharma whatsoever called "the time of cessation.
Furthermore, the Buddha taught:
"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) perish moment by moment; there is not a single moment in which they abide."
How can you say that present phenomena are both "about to cease" and "not yet about to cease"?
If you claim that within a single moment there is no such thing as being "about to cease" or "not yet about to cease," then you contradict your own doctrine.
In your Abhidharma it is said:
there are phenomena that are subject to cessation and phenomena that are not subject to cessation;
there are phenomena that one desires to cause to cease and phenomena that one does not desire to cause to cease.
Regarding dharmas that are about to cease: these are present dharmas that are on the verge of ceasing.

Regarding dharmas that are not about to cease: excluding those present dharmas that are on the verge of ceasing, all other present dharmas, as well as past, future, and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas, are called dharmas that are not about to cease.
Therefore, there is no condition as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). As for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
"As the Buddhas have taught, the true and subtle Dharma..."
"In these phenomena that lack conditions, how can there be a condition as an object?

The Buddha taught that all dharmas of the Mahāyāna—whether with form or formless, with shape or shapeless, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned—interpenetrate the nature of dharmas; all are empty, signless, and without conditions.
For example, just as the various rivers flowing into the ocean become of one single taste, the true Dharma is what is to be trusted;
that which is taught according to specific circumstances cannot be taken as the ultimate reality. Therefore, there is no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Regarding the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*):
"All phenomena lack intrinsic nature; therefore, they possess no characteristic of existence.
To say that 'this thing exists' is not tenable."
The Sūtra teaches that the twelve links of dependent origination exist because this exists, but this is not so. Why is that?
Because all phenomena arise from a multitude of conditions, they lack an inherent nature of their own. Because they lack an inherent nature of their own, they possess no characteristic of existence.
Since the characteristic of existence is absent, how can one say that "because this exists, that exists"?
Therefore, there is no dominant condition; the Buddha spoke of its existence or non-existence in accordance with the conceptualizations of ordinary beings.
Furthermore:
"Within the brief and extensive conditions, / The fruit sought cannot be found."
"If it does not exist within the causes and conditions, how can it emerge from them?
"Briefly," [this means] that the fruit does not exist within the collection of causes and conditions.
"In detail," [this means] that the fruit does not exist even within each individual condition.
If the effect does not exist within the causes and conditions, whether briefly or extensively, how can one say that the effect emerges from the causes and conditions?
Furthermore:
"If it is claimed that the effect is non-existent within the conditions, yet emerges from those very conditions;"
"Why does this fruit not arise from that which is not a condition?
If the fruit cannot be found when sought within conditions, why does it not emerge from what is not a condition?"
If there is no jar within the clay, why does it not emerge from milk?
Furthermore:
"If an effect arises from conditions, those conditions lack intrinsic nature."
Since that which lacks intrinsic nature does not arise, how could it arise from conditions?
The effect does not arise from conditions, nor does it arise from non-conditions;
because the effect does not exist, conditions and non-conditions likewise do not exist.
If a fruit arises from various conditions, those conditions lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If there is no intrinsic nature, there is no phenomenon; and if there is no phenomenon, how can it produce anything?
Therefore, a fruit does not arise from conditions.
Regarding "not arising from non-conditions": because conditions are refuted, one speaks of "non-conditions.
In reality, there is no such thing as a dharma that is a non-condition; therefore, things do not arise from non-conditions.
If they did not arise from either [conditions or non-conditions], then there would be no fruit.
Because there is no fruit, neither conditions nor non-conditions exist.
Chapter 2: Examination of the Past and Future. Verse 25. Question:
The world perceives with its eyes that activity exists in the three times.
The gone, the not-yet-gone, and the presently-going:
because there is activity, one should know that dharmas exist.
The answer is:
"There is no going in that which has already gone, nor is there going in that which has not yet gone;
apart from that which has already gone and that which has not yet gone, there is also no going in the process of going.
There is no going in that which has already gone, because it has already gone.
If going were to exist apart from that which has gone, this would not be possible.
Nor is there going in that which has not yet gone, because the dharma of going does not yet exist.
The "time of going" is defined as half-gone and half-not-yet-gone, for it is not separate from what has already gone and what has not yet gone.
Question:

"Where there is movement, there is going; within this [movement], there is the time of going, neither that which has already gone nor that which has not yet gone. Therefore, it is during the time of going that one goes."
"Wherever there is the locus of an action, therein there must be going.

We see that during the time of going (*gamyamāna*), there is the performance of the action; in what has already been gone over (*gata*), the action has ceased; and in what has not yet been gone over (*agata*), the action does not yet exist. Therefore, one should know that there is going during the time of going."
The answer is:
"How could there be the act of going within the time of going?
If one is separated from the act of going, the time of going cannot be found."
It is not the case that there is a "time of going" (gamyamāna) wherein the act of going exists. Why?
Because apart from the act of going, a time of going cannot be apprehended.
If there were a time of going apart from the act of going, then there would have to be going within that time of going, just as there are fruits within a vessel.
Furthermore:
"If one says that 'there is going during the time of going,' such a person is at fault."
"Departure exists apart from the time of departing, because at the time of departing there is only the act of departing.
If one claims that there is no departure within what has already departed or what has not yet departed, but that departure truly exists during the time of departing, such a person is at fault.
If the time of going existed apart from the act of going, they would not be mutually dependent. Why is this?
If one says that there is going during the time of going, then these would be two separate things.
But in reality this is not so; therefore, one cannot say that there is a time of going apart from the act of going.
Furthermore:
"If there were going during the time of going, then there would be two kinds of going."
"First is that which is called 'the time of going'; second is that which is called 'going during the time of going.
If one claims that there is going within the time of going, this entails the fault that there would be two goings:
first, the going by virtue of which there is a 'time of going'; [and second, the going occurring therein]."
Second, there is going within the process of going.
Question:
If there are two goings, what fault is there?
The answer is:
"If there were two acts of going, then there would be two goers;
yet apart from a goer, an act of going cannot be found."
If there were two acts of going, there would then be two goers.
Why? Because it is due to the act of going that there is a goer.
To say that one person has two goings—that is, two acts of going—is not so; therefore, there is no going even at the time of going.
[The opponent] asks:
It may be granted that there is no dharma of going apart from the goer.
Now, it is certain that there is a goer within these three times.
The response says:
"If one is separated from the goer, the act of going cannot be apprehended."
Since there is no such thing as the act of going (*gati*), how can there be a goer (*gantṛ*)?
If one is separated from the goer, then the act of going cannot be apprehended.
Now, how can you say that within the absence of the act of going, a goer definitely exists throughout the three times?
Furthermore:
"The goer does not go; the non-goer does not go.
Apart from the goer and the non-goer, there is no third goer."
There is no goer. Why is this?
If there were a goer, there would be two kinds: [the goer and the act of going].
Whether it be one who goes or one who does not go—
apart from these two, there is no third goer.
Question:
If it is the goer who goes, what fault is there?
The answer is:
"If one says that the goer goes, how can this meaning be established?"
"If one is separated from the act of going, a goer cannot be found.
If it is claimed that there definitely exists a goer who employs the act of going, this is not so.
Why is this? Because apart from the act of going, a goer cannot be apprehended.
If the act of going were definitively existent apart from the goer, then the goer could employ that act of going.
But in reality, this is not so.
Furthermore:
"If there were going for one who goes, then there would be two kinds of going."
The first refers to "the goer goes," and the second refers to "the act of going goes.
If one says that the goer employs the act of going, there are two fallacies:
within a single goer, there would be two acts of going—one by which the act of going establishes the goer, and another by which the goer establishes the act of going.
It is not the case that the goer is established first and only then employs the act of going;
therefore, the claim that within the three time periods there is a definitively existent goer who employs the act of going is incorrect.
Furthermore:
"If one says that 'the goer goes,' this person falls into error;
for there would be a goer apart from the act of going, and one speaks of a goer possessing going."
If one asserts that the goer can employ the act of going, that person is at fault, for they maintain that there is a goer apart from the act of going.
Why is this? To say that the goer employs the act of going implies that the goer exists prior to the act of going.
This is not the case; therefore, there is no goer within the three times.
Furthermore, if going and a goer were definitively existent, there would have to be an initial departure.
Yet, when seeking its arising within the three times, it cannot be found.
Why is this? "There is no arising in that which has already gone; there is no arising in that which has not yet gone."
If there is no going within the time of going, where could going possibly exist?
Why is there no going within the three times?
"There is no going in that which has not yet gone, nor is there any in that which has already gone."
These two should have an act of setting out; but if it has not yet departed, how can there be setting out?
There is no departing and no non-departing, nor is there a time of departing.
Since in all cases there is no setting out, for what reason do you make such distinctions?
If a person has not yet set out, there is neither the time of going nor that which has already been gone;
if there is setting out, it must occur within one of two states:
either the time of going or that which has already been gone.
Both cases are untenable, because there is no setting forth (prasthāna) when one has not yet departed.
How can there be setting forth within that which has not yet departed?

Since there is no setting forth, there is no departing; since there is no departing, there is no departer. How, then, could there be that which has already departed, that which has not yet departed, or the time of departing?
Question:
If there is no going and no goer, there should be staying and a stayer. Answer:
"The goer does not abide; the non-goer does not abide.
Apart from the goer and the non-goer, how could there be a third who abides?
If there were abiding and an abider, it would have to be either the goer who abides or the non-goer who abides.
If one were to depart from these two, there would have to be a third state of abiding;
however, this is not the case.
One who is moving does not abide because their motion has not yet ceased; that which is contrary to motion is termed "abiding."
That which does not go also does not abide.
Why? Because abiding exists due to the cessation of the dharma of going; where there is no going, there is no abiding.
Apart from the goer and the non-goer, there is no third who stays.
If there were a third who stays, he would be included within the category of either the goer or the non-goer.
For this reason, one cannot say that the goer stays.
Furthermore:
"If the goer were to stay, how could such a proposition be possible?"
"If one were to be separated from going, a goer could not be found.
Your claim that "the goer stays" is not tenable.
Why is this? Apart from the act of going, a goer cannot be found.
If the goer were identical with the characteristic of going, how could there be staying?
Because going and staying are mutually contradictory.
Furthermore:
"There is no staying in that which has gone or that which has not yet gone; there is also no staying in the process of going."
"All modes of activity are identical in meaning to 'going.
If one were to claim that the goer abides, that person must abide within the time of going, the already gone, or the not yet gone.
In all three cases, there is no abiding; therefore, your statement that "the goer abides" is not correct.
Just as the dharma of going and the dharma of abiding have been refuted, the same applies to walking and stopping.
"Formative activity" (*saṃskāra*) is like the continuity from a grain seed to the sprout, stem, leaves, and so forth.
"Cessation" (*nirodha*) is the cessation of the sprout, stem, and leaves because the grain seed has ceased.
It is called "activity" because it is a continuity; it is called "cessation" because it is a severance.

Furthermore, the sequence from ignorance as the condition for volitional formations up to old age and death is called "arising" (*saṃskāra*); the cessation of volitional formations and so forth due to the cessation of ignorance is called "stopping" (*nirodha*).
Question:

Although you have refuted the "goer" and the "act of going," as well as the "dweller" and the "act of dwelling," through various methods, we nonetheless see with our own eyes that there is going and dwelling.
The answer is:
That which is seen by the fleshly eye is not to be trusted.
If going and the goer truly existed, would they be established as a single dharma?
Is it established by means of two dharmas?
Both positions entail faults. Why is this so?
“That the act of going is the goer—this is not so;
that the act of going is different from the goer—this also is not so.
If the act of going and the goer were one, this would not be so; if they were different, this also would not be so.
Question: What are the faults in [the positions of] identity and difference? Answer:
If one were to say that the act of going is itself the goer,
then the agent and the action would be one and the same.
If one were to say that the act of going is distinct from the goer;
"If there is going apart from the goer, or if there is a goer apart from going"—
both of these positions entail faults. Why is this so?
If the act of going were identical to the goer, this would be a confusion that destroys the principle of dependent origination.
It is because of going that there is a goer, and it is because of a goer that there is going.
Furthermore, "going" is termed the phenomenon (*dharma*), and the "goer" is termed the person (*pudgala*). The person is permanent while the phenomenon is impermanent.
If they were one, then both would necessarily be either permanent or both impermanent.
The first [position] involves such faults as these.
If they were different, there would be a contradiction:

there would be an agent of going even when the act of going does not yet exist, and there would be the act of going even when the agent of going does not yet exist; they would not be mutually dependent, and when one phenomenon ceases, the other would still remain.
In the case of difference, there are such faults as these.
Furthermore:
"Going and the goer are two; they would be established as either identical or different phenomena."
"Since both gates are unestablished, how could there be establishment?
Whether the goer and the act of going exist as established by a single dharma or by distinct dharmas, neither can be obtained;
it has already been stated that there is no third dharma by which they could be established."
If you claim that there is establishment [of the goer], you should state the causes and conditions.
Since there is no going and no goer, we shall now explain further:
"By means of going one knows the goer; yet one cannot employ this very going."
"Since there is no going prior [to the goer], there is no goer who goes.
By what means of going could one know the goer?
That goer cannot employ this means of going.
Why is this? Because when this phenomenon of going has not yet occurred, there is no goer; likewise, there is no time of going, no having gone, and no not-yet-gone.
It is like how, only when there is first a person and a city, can there be something that arises.
The same does not hold for the act of going and the goer; for the goer is established by means of the act of going, and the act of going is established by means of the goer.
Furthermore:
"By means of going one knows the goer, but one cannot employ a going other [than that which establishes it]."
"Because within a single goer, two acts of going cannot be found.
Whichever method of going one uses to cognize the goer, that goer cannot employ a different method of going.
Why is this? Because within a single going, two acts of going cannot be found.
Furthermore:
A definitively existent goer cannot employ the three kinds of going;
a non-definitively existent goer likewise does not employ the three kinds of going.
Whether the act of going is fixed or unfixed, the goer does not employ the three.
"Therefore, the goer, the act of going, and the place to which one goes—all are non-existent.
"Determined" means that [the goer] is said to exist inherently from the beginning, not arising dependent upon the process of going.
The phenomenon of going is called bodily movement.
It is categorized into three types: that which has not yet gone, that which has already gone, and that which is in the process of going.

If a goer existed as a determinate entity, there would have to be a goer apart from the act of going, and he could not remain stationary; therefore, it is said that a determinate goer cannot employ these three modes of going.

If the goer is not determinate, that which is not determinate is said to be fundamentally non-existent. Since the goer is designated by virtue of the act of going, and because the act of going does not exist [independently], one cannot employ the three types of going.
Because of the act of going, there is a goer; if the act of going did not exist beforehand, there would be no goer.
How then can you say that the goer does not definitely employ three acts of going?
As it is with the goer, so it is with the act of going.
If the act of going were to exist independently and prior to the goer, then the act of going would not depend upon the goer; therefore, the goer cannot employ the three modes of going.
If the act of going is definitively non-existent, what use would there be for a goer?
Reflecting and examining in this way, one sees that the act of going, the goer, and the place to be gone to are all phenomena that exist in mutual dependence.

Because there is the act of going, there is a goer; because there is a goer, there is the act of going. Because of these two dharmas, there is a place to which one goes. One cannot say they definitely exist, nor can one say they definitely do not exist. Therefore, one knows with certainty that these three dharmas are illusory, empty, and non-existent; they possess only provisional names, being like a phantom or a magical creation.

Chapter Three: An Analysis of the Six Sense Faculties (Ṣaḍāyatana-parīkṣā) Question: The Sūtras speak of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatanāni*), namely: "The eye, ear, nose, tongue, Body, and mind—these are the six sense faculties. [Verse 1] The eye sees forms; the ear hears sounds; The nose smells odors; the tongue tastes flavors; The body feels tangibles; the mind knows phenomena. Thus, these six are called the "six internal bases" (*ṣaḍ-adhyātma-āyatanāni*). [Verse 2] If the eye were able to see forms by itself, Then even without the presence of light, it should be able to see. If the eye could see forms by itself, Then even in darkness, it should be able to see. [Verse 3] If the eye were able to see forms by itself, Then it would not require the assistance of light.

If the eye could see forms by itself, Then it would not require the assistance of space. [Verse 4] If the eye were able to see forms by itself, Then it would not require the assistance of consciousness. If the eye could see forms by itself, Then it would not require the assistance of attention. [Verse 5] If the eye were able to see forms by itself, Then it would not require the assistance of the visual faculty. If the eye could see forms by itself, Then it would not require the assistance of the visual organ. [Verse 6] If the eye were able to see forms by itself, Then it would not require the assistance of the visual field. If the eye could see forms by itself, Then it would not require the assistance of the object. [Verse 7] If the eye were able to see forms by itself, Then it would not require the assistance of the visual consciousness. If the eye could see forms by itself, Then it would not require the assistance of the visual cognition. [Verse 8] If the eye were able to see forms by itself, Then it would not require the assistance of the visual contact. If the eye could see forms by itself, Then it would not require the assistance of the visual sensation. Thus ends the third chapter, the Analysis of the Six Sense Faculties, from the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.
"These six faculties, such as the eye, engage with the six objects, such as form.

Herein, the eye is the internal faculty and form is the external object; the eye is able to see form, and so on, until the mind is the internal faculty and mental phenomena (dharma) are the external object; the mind is able to cognize mental phenomena.
Answer: There is none. Why is this?
"This eye cannot see its own substance;
if it cannot see itself, how can it see other things?
Thus, the eye is unable to see its own essence.
Why is this? Just as a lamp can illuminate itself and also illuminate others,
if the eye were of the nature of seeing, it should likewise see itself and see others.
In reality, however, this is not so; therefore, the verse says: "If the eye cannot see itself, how can it see other things?
A questioner asks:
"Although the eye cannot see itself, it is nonetheless able to see others."
Just as fire can burn others but cannot burn itself, the answer is:
"The analogy of fire does not apply; it is established by the phenomenon of visual perception."
"Regarding that which has gone, that which has not yet gone, and the process of going—these matters have already been answered in their entirety.
Although you employ the analogy of fire, it cannot establish the phenomenon of visual perception.

This matter has already been answered in the "Examination of Going and Coming": just as there is no going in that which has already gone, no going in that which has not yet gone, and no going in the process of going; so it is here.

Just as there is no burning in what has already been burned, what has not yet been burned, or that which is currently burning, so too there is no characteristic of seeing in what has already been seen, what has not yet been seen, or that which is currently being seen.
Furthermore:
"If seeing occurs when there is no seeing, it cannot be called seeing."
To say that the eye can see—this is not so. When the eye has not yet encountered a form, it cannot see;
at that time, it is not called "seeing. It is only because of encountering a form that it is called "seeing."
Therefore, the verse states: "When not seeing, there is no seeing. How, then, can one see by means of seeing?
Furthermore, in both cases, the act of seeing is absent. Why is this so?
"Seeing cannot see, nor does non-seeing see;
if seeing has already been refuted, then the seer is also refuted.
Seeing cannot see, because this has already been explained above.
It is neither seeing nor non-seeing, because it lacks the characteristic of seeing.
If there is no characteristic of seeing, how can there be the ability to see?
Since the dharma of seeing does not exist, the seer also does not exist.
Why is this? If there were a seer apart from seeing, then even one without eyes should see by means of another sense-faculty.
If seeing sees, then there must be the characteristic of seeing within seeing itself.
The seer has no characteristic of seeing; therefore, the verse says: "If seeing is already refuted, then the seer is refuted.
Furthermore:
"Whether apart from seeing or not apart from seeing, a seer cannot be found."
Since there is no seer, how can there be seeing or an object seen?
If there is seeing, the seer is not established;
if there is no seeing, the seer is likewise not established.
Since the seer does not exist, how can there be seeing or that which is seen?
If there is no seer, who could employ the act of seeing to discern external forms?
Therefore, the verse says: "Because there is no seer, how can there be seeing or that which is seen?"
Furthermore:
"Because seeing and the seen do not exist, the four factors beginning with consciousness do not exist;
how then could the various conditions, such as the four graspings, possibly exist?"
Because seeing and the objects of sight do not exist, the four dharmas of consciousness, contact, feeling, and craving are all non-existent.
Because craving and the others are absent, the twelve links of dependent origination, such as the four types of clinging and so forth, are likewise non-existent.
Furthermore: "The ear,
nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as sound and the hearer—
know that these meanings are all the same as what was explained above."

Just as the seeing [faculty] and the visible [objects] are empty because they depend on various conditions and thus lack any fixed nature, one should know that the other five sense organs—the ear and so forth—and the five sense objects—sound and so forth—are likewise identical to the seeing and the visible. Because their meaning is the same, they are not explained separately.
Chapter Four: An Examination of the Five Aggregates (Pañcaskandha-parīkṣā). Nine verses. Question:
The Sūtras state that there are five aggregates (*skandhas*). How is this so?
The answer is:
"If one is separated from the cause of form, then form cannot be apprehended;
if one were to be separated from form, then the cause of form could not be apprehended."
Regarding the cause of form: it is like cloth being caused by threads; if the threads are removed, there is no cloth, and if the cloth is removed, there are no threads.
Cloth is like form, and the threads are like the cause.
Question:
If form existed apart from the causes of form, what fault would there be? Answer:
"If form exists apart from the cause of form, then that form would be without a cause.
That there could be a phenomenon without a cause—such a thing is not possible.
It would be like there being cloth apart from the threads; the cloth would then be without a cause.
There is no phenomenon in the world that exists without a cause.
Question:
Within the teachings of the Buddha, the teachings of non-Buddhists, and worldly conventions, there are all those phenomena that lack a cause.
In the Buddha-dharma, there are three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); because they are unconditioned and eternal, they have no cause.
In the systems of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), there are such things as space (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), direction (*dis*), the self (*ātman*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa*).
Worldly phenomena such as space, time, and direction—these three dharmas are called "eternal" because there is no place where they do not exist; being eternal, they have no cause.
Why, then, do you say that a causeless dharma does not exist in the world?
Answer: This doctrine of causelessness is merely a verbal expression; when subjected to analytical reflection, it is entirely non-existent.
If a phenomenon arises from causes and conditions, one should not say it is causeless.
If there were no causes and conditions, it would be as I have said. Question:
There are two kinds of causes:
The first is the cause of action; the second is the cause of verbal expression.
This dharma of no-cause lacks a cause of action, but possesses only a cause of verbal expression for the purpose of making it known to others.
The answer is:
although there are verbal arguments for this, the matter is not so.
Space has already been refuted among the six elements; the remaining matters shall be refuted later.
Furthermore, if even manifest phenomena can all be refuted, how much more so the invisible dharmas such as atoms?
Therefore, it is said that there are no causeless dharmas in the world.
Question:
If there were a cause of form that exists apart from form itself, what fault would there be? Answer:
"If there were a cause for form apart from form itself, it would be a cause without a fruit;
to say there is a cause without a fruit is impossible.
If one were to exclude the fruit of form while maintaining only the cause of form, that would indeed be a cause without a fruit.
Question:
If there were causes without effects, what fault would there be? Answer:
There is no such thing in the world as a cause without an effect.
Why is this? It is because it is called a "cause" precisely because of the effect.
If there is no effect, how can it be called a cause?
Furthermore, if the effect does not exist within the cause, why do things not arise from what is not a cause?
This matter is as explained in the "Refutation of Causes and Conditions" chapter.
Therefore, there is no cause that lacks an effect.
Furthermore:
"If form already exists, then it does not require a cause for form."
"If form does not exist, it likewise does not employ the cause of form.
It is not the case that there is a cause of form in both locations.
If form already existed within the prior cause, it could not be called the "cause of form."
If form does not previously exist within the cause, it cannot be called the cause of form. Question:
If both cases are untenable, and there is merely form without a cause, what fault is there?
The answer is:
"That form exists without a cause—this can never be so.
Therefore, the wise should not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding form."
"If it is already impossible for an effect to exist within a cause or not to exist within a cause, how much more so for there to be form without a cause?
Therefore, it is said: 'That there is form without a cause—this is ultimately not the case.'"
Therefore, those who possess wisdom should not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding form (*rūpa*).

Conceptual discrimination is the mark of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); through the defilement of ignorance and craving, they become greedily attached to form, and subsequently give rise to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) based on false views, asserting such things as "the effect exists within the cause" or "the effect does not exist within the cause."
Now, within this, form cannot be found when sought; therefore, the wise should not engage in conceptual discrimination.
Furthermore:
"If the effect were similar to the cause, this would not be so."
"If the fruit were not similar to the cause, this matter would also be untenable.
If the fruit were similar to the cause, this matter would likewise be untenable, because the cause is subtle while the fruit is coarse.

The causes and effects differ in their form, power, and other attributes; for instance, if cloth were identical to its threads, it would not be called "cloth," because the threads are many while the cloth is one.
Therefore, one cannot say that cause and effect are similar.
If it were the case that cause and effect are dissimilar, this would also be incorrect.
For instance, hemp fibers do not produce silk, and coarse yarn does not yield fine cloth; therefore, one cannot say that cause and effect are dissimilar.
Since these two positions are untenable, there is neither form nor a cause for form.
"The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregates of mental formations and consciousness,
and all other phenomena, are in every respect the same as the aggregate of form."
The four aggregates and all phenomena should likewise be analyzed and deconstructed through such contemplation.
Furthermore, the author of this treatise, wishing to praise the meaning of emptiness, speaks this verse:
"If someone should ask a question, And one wishes to answer apart from emptiness,"
This would not constitute a valid answer, for it shares the same doubt as the original.
If someone raises an objection and speaks of its faults while departing from emptiness,
this does not constitute a valid objection, for it likewise shares the same doubt as the original.

If, during a debate, each party maintains their own fixed position and engages in questioning and answering apart from the meaning of emptiness, neither constitutes a valid dialogue; both parties remain equally in doubt.
As when someone says,
"A jar is impermanent," the questioner asks:
"Why is it impermanent? He replied,
"Because it arises from impermanent causes."
"This is not called an answer.
Why? Because there is still doubt regarding the causes and conditions, as one does not know whether they are permanent or impermanent."
This is because it shares the same doubt as the opponent.
If the questioner wishes to point out the fault [in the opponent's position] but explains the impermanence of all phenomena without relying on emptiness, then it cannot be called a valid critique.
Why is this? You use impermanence to refute my permanence, and I likewise use permanence to refute your impermanence.
If things were truly impermanent, there would be no karmic retribution; for the various dharmas such as the eyes and ears would perish moment by moment, and there would be no discernment.
Because there are such faults as these, none of them constitute valid objections; they are identical to the very doubts [the opponent] holds.
If one refutes permanence by relying on emptiness, then there is no fault. Why is this?

Because this person does not grasp at the mark of emptiness, even when engaging in question and answer, one must still rely upon the dharma of emptiness; how much more so for one who seeks the mark of nirvana—the cessation of suffering.
Chapter Five: Examination of the Six Elements. Five verses. Question:
Each of the six elements possesses a fixed characteristic; because they possess fixed characteristics, there are therefore six elements.
The answer is:
"When the characteristic of emptiness does not yet exist, there is no phenomenon of space;
if space existed prior [to that characteristic], it would then be without characteristics."
If the dharma of space existed prior to the characteristic of space, then space would be without characteristics.
Why is this? Because the absence of form is what is called the characteristic of space.
Form is a conditioned phenomenon and is impermanent; if form has not yet arisen, then since it has not arisen, there is no cessation, and at that time the characteristic of space does not exist.
It is because of form that there is the sphere of non-form; this sphere of non-form is called the characteristic of space.
Question:
If there were empty space without characteristics, what fault would there be? Answer:
"This dharma of signlessness does not exist anywhere;
within the dharma of signlessness, signs have nothing to characterize.
If one seeks the dharma of signlessness among dharmas that are either permanent or impermanent, it cannot be found.
As the proponent says, regarding existence and non-existence, how is one to know their respective characteristics?

Therefore, arising, abiding, and ceasing are the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), while the absence of arising, abiding, and ceasing is the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If space were without characteristics, then there would be no space.
If it is claimed that it was first without characteristics and later characteristics came to characterize it, this is also not so.
If it were first without characteristics, then there would be no dharma that could be characterized.
Why is this? "Within both the characterized and the uncharacterized, the characteristic has no place to abide;
apart from the characterized and the uncharacterized, it abides nowhere else."
For instance, having humps, horns, hair at the end of the tail, and a dewlap hanging from the neck—these are called the characteristics of an ox.
If one is devoid of these characteristics, there is no ox.
If there were no ox, these various characteristics would have nothing in which to abide.
Therefore, it is said that within the dharma of signlessness (*animitta*), a characteristic has nothing upon which to characterize.
Furthermore, a characteristic does not abide within a characterized thing (*nimitta*), because that characterized thing already exists [prior to the characteristic].

Just as the characteristic of fire does not abide within the characteristic of water because it possesses its own intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), so too, if a characteristic were to abide within that which lacks characteristics, it would be without cause; and that which is without cause is called a non-existent thing (*abhāva*) that nonetheless possesses a characteristic.
The characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the characterized (*lakṣya*), and the characteristic of permanence exist because they depend upon one another.
Apart from the dharmas of having characteristics and lacking characteristics, there is no third locus that can be characterized.
Therefore, the verse says: "Apart from having characteristics and lacking characteristics, it does not abide elsewhere either."
Furthermore: "Because the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) does not exist, the characterized (*lakṣya*) also does not exist;
because the characterized does not exist, the defining characteristic likewise does not exist."
Because marks have no place of abiding, there are no dharmas that can be marked;
because there are no dharmas that can be marked, the dharma of marking also does not exist. Why is this?
Because there are characteristics (lakṣaṇa) due to the characterized (lakṣya), and because there is the characterized due to the characteristics; they exist through mutual dependence.
"Therefore, now that there are no characteristics, There is also no characterized object;
Once characteristics and the characterized are transcended, There is furthermore no entity whatsoever."
When one investigates the beginning and end within causes and conditions, neither the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) nor the characterized (*lakṣya*) can be definitively found.
Because these two cannot be found, all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-existent.

All phenomena are subsumed within the two categories of the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and that which possesses the characteristic (*lakṣya*); sometimes the characteristic serves as that which possesses the characteristic, and sometimes that which possesses the characteristic serves as the characteristic.
For example, fire has smoke as its characteristic, and smoke likewise has fire as its characteristic.
Question:
If existence does not exist, then non-existence ought to exist. Answer:
"If existence itself does not exist, how could non-existence exist?
Since both existence and non-existence are absent, who is it that knows existence and non-existence?
Whether a thing perishes by itself or is destroyed by another, this is called non-existence.
Nothing exists without having arisen from existence; it is from existence that existence comes to be.
Therefore it is said: "If there were no existence, how could there be non-existence?
Since even seeing with the eyes or hearing with the ears cannot be apprehended, how much more so the case of non-existent things?
Question:
Since existence does not exist, non-existence also does not exist; therefore, there ought to be one who knows both existence and non-existence.
Answer:
If there were a knower, would they exist within existence or within non-existence?
Since both existence and non-existence have been refuted, the knower is likewise refuted.
Therefore, know that space is neither existent nor non-existent.
"It is neither characteristic nor that which possesses characteristics; the remaining five are likewise like space.
Just as various searches for the characteristics of space cannot find them, so it is with the other five elements.
Question: Space is neither at the beginning nor at the end.
Why is it refuted first? Answer:
Earth, water, fire, and wind are easily broken because they are a combination of various conditions.
Consciousness is easily broken because it perceives impermanence and change through the causes of suffering and pleasure.
Space possesses no such characteristics; it is only because ordinary beings desire it to exist that it is refuted first.

Furthermore, space can sustain the four great elements, and through the causes and conditions of the four great elements, consciousness arises; therefore, by refuting the root first, the others are refuted of their own accord.
Question:
All people in the world perceive that all phenomena exist or do not exist; why do you alone contradict the world by saying that there is nothing seen?
The answer is:
"Those of shallow wisdom perceive all phenomena as having either the mark of existence or non-existence;
they are thus unable to see the dharma of peace that extinguishes such views."

If a person has not yet attained the Way and does not perceive the true reality of all phenomena (*dharmas*), they engage in various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) due to the causes and conditions of craving and views.
When they see a phenomenon arise, they say it "exists," grasping at its marks and asserting existence;
when they see a phenomenon perish, they say it is "annihilated," grasping at its marks and asserting non-existence.

The wise person perceives that as all phenomena arise, they immediately cease, thereby eliminating the view of non-existence; they perceive that as all phenomena cease, they eliminate the view of existence. Therefore, although they have perceptions regarding all phenomena, these are all like illusions and dreams; even the perception of the untainted path is extinguished, let alone other views.
Therefore, if one does not see cessation but sees a dharma of security, then one sees existence and non-existence.
Chapter Six: An Analysis of Passion and the One Who Passions. Verse 10. Question:
The Sūtras state that desire, hatred, and delusion are the roots of the world.

Greed has various names: first it is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*), next it is called attachment (*graha*), next it is called defilement (*saṃkleśa*), next it is called sexual desire (*maithunecchā*), and next it is called greed (*lobha*); such are its names.
These are the fetters (*saṃyojana*); that which relies upon sentient beings is called the "one who is defiled," while craving (*rāga*) is called the "defiling dharma.
Because there is both the defiling dharma and the one who is defiled, there is craving.
The other two are likewise: where there is hatred, there is one who hates; where there is delusion, there is one who is deluded.

By means of these three poisons as causes and conditions, the three types of karma arise; by means of the three types of karma as causes and conditions, the three realms arise. Therefore, all phenomena exist.
Answer: Although the sutras speak of the names of the three poisons, when sought in reality, they cannot be found. Why is this?
"If there were a defiled person existing prior to and independent of the defiled phenomena,
then because of that defiled person, the defiled phenomena would have to arise.
But if there is no defiled person, how could there be defilement?"
"Whether there is defilement or not, the defiler is likewise so.
If the defiler were already definitively existent prior to defilement, then further defilement would not be required, because the defiler would have already been defiled.
If the defiled person did not exist prior to the defilement, then defilement itself should not arise; rather, it must first be that there is a defiled person before defilement arises.
If there were no defiled person beforehand, then there would be no one to undergo defilement.
The same applies to the defilements (*kleśa*): if the defilements were to exist independently prior to the person, they would be without a cause; how then could they arise?
It would be like fire without fuel.
If defiled phenomena were definitively non-existent beforehand, then there would be no defiler; therefore, the verse says: "Whether defilement exists or does not exist, the defiler is likewise."
Question: If it is impossible for the defiled phenomenon and the defiler to arise in mutual dependence as prior and posterior,
what fault is there if they were to arise simultaneously?
The answer is:
"The defiler and the act of defiling cannot both be established simultaneously;
if the defiler and the act of defiling were simultaneous, they would lack mutual dependence."
If the defiled phenomenon and the defiler were established simultaneously, they would not depend upon one another;

the defiled phenomenon would not exist because of the defiler, nor would the defiler exist because of the defiled phenomenon. These two would consequently be eternal, as they would have been established without causes.
If [the self] were permanent, there would be many faults, and there would be no dharma of liberation.
Furthermore, we shall now refute the defiled phenomena and the defiled agent by means of the analysis of identity and difference. Why is this?
"If the stained one and the staining dharma are one, how can one dharma be joined?
If the stained one and the staining dharma are different, how can different dharmas be joined?
Whether the staining dharma and the stained one are joined as one dharma or joined as different dharmas.
If there were oneness, there would be no conjunction. Why is this?
How can a single dharma conjoin with itself?
Just as the tip of a finger cannot touch itself,
it is likewise impossible for it to conjoin with a different dharma. Why is this so?
Because they are established as distinct.
If each were already fully established, there would be no need for them to combine; even if they were to combine, they would still remain distinct.
Furthermore, both identity and difference are untenable.
Why is this? "If identity were to combine, there would be combination even apart from its associates;
if difference were to combine, there would likewise be combination even apart from its associates."

If passion (*rāga*) and the impassioned one (*rakta*) were identical, yet were forcibly designated as "conjoined," then passion and the impassioned one would exist independently of other causal conditions.
Furthermore, if they were identical, there should not be two distinct names—passion and the impassioned one; for passion is a phenomenon (*dharma*), while the impassioned one is a person (*pudgala*).
If person and phenomena were one, there would be great confusion.
If passion and the impassioned were distinct yet said to be conjoined, then their conjunction would not require any further causes or conditions.
If things that are distinct were to combine, then even those that are distant should combine.
Question: It may be granted that two identical things do not combine; however—
The eye sees the conjunction of distinct phenomena.
He replied:
"If there were conjunction between distinct things, what would be the relationship between the defilement and the defiled one?"
"These two characteristics must first be distinct, and only then can one speak of their combined characteristic.
If the defilement and the defiled subject were first established as having a definitive distinction and only later joined, then they could not be joined.
Why is this? These two characteristics were already distinct prior to their being forcibly asserted as conjoined.
Furthermore:
"If the passion and the one who possesses passion were each established as having distinct characteristics beforehand,
then since they have already been established as having distinct characteristics, how can you say they are joined?
If passion and the one who possesses passion were each established as separate characteristics beforehand, why do you now insist on asserting that they have the characteristic of being joined?"
Furthermore:
"Since distinct characteristics cannot be established, you therefore seek to conjoin them;
yet since the characteristic of conjunction is ultimately unestablished, you speak again of distinct characteristics."
Since the distinct characteristics of passion and the impassioned one have not been established, you further assert the characteristic of their conjunction.
However, there is a fault within this characteristic of conjunction; thus, neither passion nor the impassioned one is established.
In order to establish the characteristic of conjunction, you further speak of the characteristic of difference.
You yourself have established a fixed [position], yet what you have stated is not fixed. Why is this?
"Since the characteristic of difference is not established, the characteristic of conjunction is likewise not established;
within what characteristic of difference could one wish to speak of a characteristic of conjunction?
Because the characteristic of difference between the defilement and the defiled one is not established herein, the characteristic of conjunction is also not established.
In what distinct characteristic (*bhinnalakṣaṇa*) do you wish to speak of a characteristic of conjunction (*saṃyogalakṣaṇa*)?
Furthermore:
"In this way, the defilement and the defiled one are neither conjoined nor non-conjoined."
All phenomena are likewise: they are neither formed through conjunction nor formed without conjunction.
As it is with attachment, so it is with hatred and delusion.
As it is with the three poisons, so it is with all afflictions and all phenomena.
Neither prior nor posterior, neither joined nor dispersed, and so forth; it is established through causes and conditions.
*Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, Fascicle One;
*Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, Fascicle Two.
Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, with commentary by the Brahmin Qingmu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter Seven: An Analysis of the Three Characteristics. Thirty-five verses. Question:
The Sūtras state that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) have three characteristics:
arising (*jāti*), abiding (*sthiti*), and ceasing (*bhanga*).
All things arise through the characteristic of arising, abide through the characteristic of abiding, and cease through the characteristic of ceasing; therefore, all phenomena exist.
Answer: It is not so. Why is this?
Since the three characteristics lack determinacy,
are these three characteristics conditioned and capable of acting as the characteristics of the conditioned,
or are they unconditioned and yet capable of acting as the characteristics of the conditioned?
Neither of these two positions is tenable. Why?
"If arising were conditioned, it would necessarily possess the three characteristics."
If arising were unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), how could it be called a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*)?
If arising were conditioned, it would necessarily possess the three characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing;
however, this is not the case.
Why is this? Because they are mutually contradictory.
To be contradictory means that arising corresponds to phenomena that arise, abiding corresponds to phenomena that abide, and ceasing corresponds to phenomena that cease.
When a phenomenon arises, there should not be the characteristics of abiding and cessation, which are mutually contradictory.
It is not possible for them to exist simultaneously, just as light and darkness do not coexist.
For this reason, arising should not be a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
The characteristics of duration and cessation should also be understood in this same way. Question:
If arising were not conditioned, and if it were unconditioned, what fault would there be?
Answer: If arising were unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), how could it serve as a characteristic for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*)? Why is this so?

Because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), they are called "unconditioned" by virtue of the cessation of the conditioned; therefore, it is said that non-arising and non-ceasing constitute the characteristic of the unconditioned, and they possess no further self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, a non-existent dharma cannot serve as a characteristic for a dharma, just as a rabbit’s horn or a tortoise’s hair cannot serve as a characteristic for a dharma.
For this reason, arising is not unconditioned;
abiding and cessation are likewise so.
Furthermore:
"If the three characteristics were to aggregate or disperse, they could not characterize anything;
how could the three characteristics exist in a single place at one time?"
Do these characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing each individually function as the characteristic of conditioned phenomena?
Or do they function as the characteristic of conditioned phenomena through their combination?
Both [positions] are untenable.

Why? If one asserts that they occur individually, then within a single moment there would either be the characteristic of existence or the characteristic of non-existence; at the time of arising there would be neither abiding nor ceasing, at the time of abiding there would be neither arising nor ceasing, and at the time of ceasing there would be neither arising nor abiding.
If they were to coexist in combination, how could mutually contradictory factors exist simultaneously?
Furthermore, it is not the case that these three characteristics themselves possess further three characteristics.
Why is this? "If one claims that arising, abiding, and ceasing possess further conditioned characteristics, this would lead to an infinite regress; if they do not, then they are not conditioned."

If it is claimed that arising, abiding, and ceasing possess further conditioned characteristics (saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa)—such that arising itself has further arising, abiding, and ceasing—then these three characteristics would themselves require further characteristics. If that were the case, there would be an infinite regress.

If there were no further characteristics, these three characteristics would not be called conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), nor could they function as the characteristics of conditioned phenomena.
Question: You say that the three characteristics lead to an infinite regress.
This is not so. Although arising, abiding, and ceasing are conditioned phenomena, they are not infinite. Why is this?
"That which gives rise to arising arises from that original arising;
that which is given rise to by original arising, in turn gives rise to arising.
When a phenomenon arises, it arises together with its own essence and seven other factors.
First, arising; second, abiding; third, cessation; fourth, the arising of arising; fifth, the abiding of abiding; sixth, the cessation of cessation.
Among these seven dharmas, primary arising—excluding its own self-substance—is able to give rise to the other six dharmas.

The "arising of arising" (jāti-jāti) can give rise to the "original arising" (mūla-jāti), and the "original arising" can give rise to the "arising of arising"; therefore, although these three characteristics are conditioned (saṃskṛta), they do not lead to an infinite regress.
The answer says:
"If it is claimed that this 'arising of arising' can give rise to the 'original arising';"
If arising from arising is produced from primary arising, how can it produce primary arising?
If arising from arising were able to produce primary arising, then that "arising from arising" would not be called "produced from primary arising."
Why is this? This "birth of birth" arises from the "original birth"; how then could it give rise to the original birth?
Furthermore:
"If you claim that this 'original production' (mūlotpāda) can produce 'the production of production' (utpādasyotpāda),
