then since the original production arises from that [production of production], how could it produce the production of production?
If you claim that the original production can produce the production of production, then this original production cannot be said to arise from the production of production.
Why is this? This original production arises from the production of production; how, then, can it produce that production of production?
According to the nature of the production of production, it ought to produce the original production.
Now, the "arising of arising" cannot give rise to the "original arising," for since the "arising of arising" lacks its own intrinsic nature, how could it give rise to the original arising?
Therefore, the original arising cannot give rise to the arising of arising.
Question:

When this "birth of birth" arises, it does not produce the "original birth" either before or after; rather, it is only at the very moment the "birth of birth" arises that it can produce the original birth.
Answer:
Not so. Why? "If the 'birth of birth' at the time of its arising could produce the 'original birth';"
"If 'the production of production' has not yet come into being, how can it produce 'the production of the producer'?

If you claim that when "the production of production" arises, it can produce "the production of the producer," that might be so; however, in reality, it does not yet exist. Therefore, at the time "the production of production" arises, it cannot produce "the production of the producer."
Furthermore:
"If the 'arising of the primary arising' (mūlotpādotpāda), upon its own arising, could give rise to the 'arising of the arising' (utpādotpāda);
since the primary arising has not yet come into being, how could it give rise to the arising of the arising?"

If it is claimed that when this "arising of arising" (utpādasyotpādaḥ) arises, it can give rise to the "arising of arising," that may be so; however, since it does not yet exist [at that time], the "arising of arising" cannot, at the moment of its own arising, give rise to the "arising of arising."
Question:
"Just as a lamp can illuminate itself and also illuminate others, so too is it with the nature of arising:
it arises from itself and causes others to arise."
"Just as a lamp enters a dark room, illuminating all objects and also illuminating itself, so too is birth:
it can produce that [other thing] and also produce itself."
Answer: It is not so. Why is this?
“There is no darkness within the lamp itself, nor is there darkness in the place where it abides.
To dispel darkness is what is called ‘illumination’; where there is no darkness, there is no illumination.
This is because the substance of the lamp itself contains no darkness, and there is likewise no darkness in the area reached by its light, for light and darkness are mutually exclusive.

It is called "illumination" because it destroys darkness; where there is no darkness, there is no illumination. How, then, can one say that a lamp illuminates itself and also illuminates others? Question:

This lamp does not illuminate before it has arisen, nor does it illuminate once it has already arisen; rather, at the very moment the lamp arises, it is able to illuminate itself and also illuminate others.
The answer is:
"How can a lamp, at the very moment it arises, destroy darkness?
When this lamp first arises, it cannot yet reach the darkness."
When a lamp is first produced, it is called "half-produced and half-unproduced. Since the substance of the lamp is not yet fully accomplished, how could it destroy darkness?
Furthermore, the lamp cannot reach the darkness; one is said to "destroy" a thief only when one has actually caught him.
If it is claimed that although the lamp does not reach the darkness, it is nevertheless able to dispel it, this too is not so.
Why? "If the lamp, without having reached the darkness, were able to dispel it," [it would follow that it could dispel all darkness everywhere].
"If the lamp is here, it destroys all darkness.
If the lamp possesses such power that it can destroy darkness without reaching it,
then lighting a lamp in this place should destroy the darkness of all places, for [the darkness] is equally beyond its reach.
Furthermore, a lamp should neither illuminate itself nor illuminate others. Why?
"If a lamp can illuminate itself, it can also illuminate others."
"Darkness should also darken itself, and it can also darken others.
Just as a lamp, because it is contrary to darkness, can illuminate itself and illuminate others.
Because darkness and light are mutually exclusive, darkness should likewise obscure itself and obscure that [light].
If darkness and light are mutually exclusive, then darkness cannot obscure itself nor obscure that [light].
Likewise, since light and darkness are mutually exclusive, light should neither illuminate itself nor illuminate that [darkness].
Therefore, the analogy of the lamp is incorrect, as the refutation of the causes and conditions for arising has not yet been exhausted; it shall now be further explained:
"If this arising has not yet arisen, how can it arise of itself?"
If arising arises from itself, once it has already arisen, what need is there for it to arise again?
When this arising arises by itself, does it arise having already arisen,
or does it arise not yet having arisen?
If that which has not yet arisen were to arise, it would be a non-existent dharma; how could a non-existent dharma arise of itself?
If one claims that what has already arisen arises, then it is already accomplished and need not arise again, just as that which has already been made should not be made again.
Whether already arisen or not yet arisen, both are non-arising; therefore, there is no arising.
Your previous statement that arising is like a lamp, which can arise from itself and cause others to arise, is incorrect;
the same applies to abiding and ceasing.
Furthermore:
"Arising does not arise from what has already arisen, nor does it arise from what has not yet arisen;
it does not arise even at the time of arising, as has already been answered regarding the past and the future."

"Arising" is designated as the coming-to-be through the conjunction of various conditions. Since there is no activity within that which has already arisen, there is no arising; since there is no activity within that which has not yet arisen, there is no arising.

It is likewise not the case for the time of arising: apart from the dharma that arises, the time of arising cannot be apprehended; and apart from the time of arising, the dharma that arises cannot be apprehended. How, then, could there be arising at the time of arising?
This matter has already been answered in the [Examination of] "Going and Coming.
A dharma that has already arisen cannot arise. Why is this?
Having arisen, it arises again; thus proceeding by succession, it would be infinite, like performing an action and then performing it again.
Furthermore, if that which has already arisen were to arise once more, by what dharma of arising would it arise?
If this characteristic of arising has not yet arisen,
yet one says that it has already arisen, then one contradicts what one has said oneself. Why is this?
The characteristic of arising has not yet arisen, yet you claim it arises.
If that which has not yet arisen is said to arise, then a phenomenon would either arise after having already arisen, or it would arise while still unarisen.
What you previously stated—that "the already-arisen arises"—is therefore not definitive.

Furthermore, just as that which has been burned should not be burned again, and that which has gone should not go again, for such reasons as these, that which has already arisen should not arise again.
A phenomenon that has not yet arisen does not arise either. Why is this?

If a phenomenon has not yet arisen, it cannot enter into conjunction with the conditions for arising; and if it does not enter into conjunction with the conditions for arising, the phenomenon cannot come into existence.

If a phenomenon were to arise without having conjoined with the conditions for its arising, then there would be acting without the phenomenon of action, going without the phenomenon of going, being defiled without the phenomenon of defilement, being angry without the phenomenon of anger, and being deluded without the phenomenon of delusion.
In this way, all worldly conventions would be subverted; therefore, an unarisen phenomenon does not arise.

Furthermore, if an unarisen phenomenon were to arise, then all unarisen phenomena in the world should arise: the bodhi of all ordinary beings, which has not yet arisen, should now arise; an Arhat of the non-retrogressive type, who possesses no afflictions, should now give rise to afflictions; and rabbits and other such creatures, which have no horns, should all now produce horns.
However, this is not the case; therefore, even unarisen dharmas do not arise. Question: Why do unarisen dharmas not arise?

It is because they have not yet attained conditions (*pratyaya*), lack volitional action (*kriyā*), lack an agent (*kartṛ*), and lack time (*kāla*) and direction (*deśa*), and for these reasons they do not arise.
If there are conditions, activity, an agent, time, place, and so forth, through their conjunction, unarisen phenomena arise.
Therefore, the claim that all unarisen phenomena never arise is not correct.
The answer is:

If a phenomenon arises through the conjunction of conditions, time, location, and so forth, it does not arise from what previously existed, nor does it arise from what previously did not exist, nor does it arise from both existence and non-existence.
The three types [of production] have already been refuted; therefore, that which has already arisen does not arise.
That which has not yet arisen does not arise, nor does that which is in the process of arising arise. Why is this so?
That which has already arisen does not arise, nor does that which has not yet arisen arise, as previously answered.
Furthermore, if there were an "arising-time" distinct from arising itself, then it would be that at the arising-time, arising occurs.
Since there is no time of arising apart from arising itself, therefore, even at the time of arising, there is no arising.
Furthermore, if one says that there is arising at the time of arising, there is the fault of a double arising: first, it is called the "time of arising" because of the act of arising;
[the second would be the arising that occurs at that time].
Second, [the claim] that arising occurs during the time of arising—
both of these are untenable.
Since there are not two dharmas, how could there be two arisings?
Therefore, that which is in the process of arising does not arise.
Furthermore, as long as the dharma of arising has not yet manifested, there is no "time of arising. Since this time of arising does not exist, upon what could the arising depend?
Therefore, one cannot say that it arises at the time of arising.

Investigating in this manner, there is no arising in that which has already arisen, no arising in that which has not yet arisen, and no arising in the process of arising. Because there is no arising, arising is not established; because arising is not established, abiding and ceasing are likewise not established.
Since arising, abiding, and ceasing are not established, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are not established.
Therefore, it has already been answered within the verse regarding going, that which has gone, and the time of going.
Question:

I do not state definitively that arising has already arisen, that it has not yet arisen, or that it arises at the very moment of arising; rather, arising occurs simply because of the conjunction of various conditions.
He replied:
"Although you have this explanation, it is nonetheless not so."
Why is this? "If one says that arising occurs at the time of arising, this matter is already unestablished;
how then can there be arising when the various conditions have converged?"

"Arising is refuted by various causes and conditions both at the time of arising and once it has arisen; why do you now further claim that arising occurs because of the conjunction of various conditions?
Whether the various conditions are complete or incomplete, they are all refuted in the same manner as arising."
Furthermore:
"If a phenomenon arises from a multitude of conditions, it is of the nature of quiescence;
therefore, both that which arises and the time of arising are quiescent."

"Phenomena born of multiple conditions lack intrinsic nature and are therefore quiescent; this quiescence is termed 'neither this nor that,' being signless, cutting off the path of language, and extinguishing all conceptual proliferation."
The term "conditioned by various causes" means that cloth exists because of threads, and a mat exists because of reeds.
If the threads possessed a fixed, inherent nature, they should not emerge from hemp;
if the cloth possessed a fixed, inherent nature, it should not emerge from the threads.
In reality, cloth exists because of threads, and threads exist because of hemp; therefore, threads lack a fixed nature, and cloth likewise lacks a fixed nature.

Just as fire and fuel are produced through the conjunction of causes and conditions and possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), so too, in the absence of fuel, fire does not exist, and in the absence of fire, fuel does not exist.

All phenomena are likewise thus; therefore, dharmas arising from a multitude of conditions lack intrinsic nature. Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty, like a mirage which has no reality.
Therefore, the verse states that both "arising" and "the time of arising" are equally quiescent; one should not say that "arising arises at the time of arising.

Although you employ various causes and conditions in an attempt to establish the characteristic of arising, these are all mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and do not constitute the characteristic of quiescence.
Question: It is certain that there are distinctions between the three periods of time.
Phenomena of the future period arise when their causes and conditions are met.
Why is it said that there is no arising?
The answer is:
"If there were any phenomena that had not yet arisen, one could say that there is arising."
"This phenomenon already existed previously; what further need is there for it to arise?
If a phenomenon that has not yet arisen in the future were to arise, since that phenomenon already existed previously, what need would there be for it to arise again?
There are dharmas that should not arise again.
Question:
Although they exist in the future, they do not possess the characteristics of the present; it is because of the characteristics of the present that one speaks of "arising."
Answer: The characteristic of the present does not exist within the future. If it does not exist, how can one say that "a dharma of the future arises"?
If it does exist, it cannot be called the future; it should be called the present, and what is present should not arise again.
Since both are non-arising, there is no arising.
Furthermore, you claim that at the time of arising, arising itself can also produce that [object].
This shall now be further explained.
"If one says that when arising arises, it is capable of producing something;
how could there be another arising that is able to produce this arising?
If the arising of arising can produce that [primary arising], then what else can produce this arising of arising?
"If one claims there is yet another arising, then arising would be infinite;
if there were an arising apart from the 'arising of arising,' then all phenomena could arise by themselves.
If there were an arising for arising, then arising would be infinite.
If that which has already arisen were to arise again by itself, then all phenomena would likewise be able to arise by themselves; yet in reality, this is not so.
Furthermore:
"An existent phenomenon should not arise, nor should a non-existent one arise."
"Neither existence nor non-existence arises; this point has already been explained previously.
Regarding all that arises, does an existent phenomenon arise, or does a non-existent phenomenon arise?
Is there arising for that which exists or for that which does not exist?
Neither is the case, as this matter has already been explained previously.
Apart from these three possibilities, there is no further arising; therefore, there is no arising.
Furthermore:
"If all phenomena are at the time of ceasing, they should not arise at that time;
if phenomena were not ceasing, this situation would never exist."
If a dharma possesses the characteristic of cessation, that dharma should not arise.
Why? Because the two characteristics are mutually contradictory.
First is the characteristic of cessation, which is the knowledge that dharmas are ceasing;
first is the characteristic of arising, which is the knowledge that dharmas are arising.
These two characteristics are mutually contradictory and cannot exist simultaneously; therefore, a dharma characterized by cessation should not arise.
Question:
If a phenomenon characterized by cessation should not arise, then a phenomenon characterized by non-cessation should arise. Answer:
Because all conditioned phenomena perish from moment to moment, there is no phenomenon that does not perish.
Apart from the conditioned, there is no determinate unconditioned phenomenon.
Unconditioned phenomena exist only as names; therefore, when it is said that there is a "non-perishing phenomenon," in the end, such a thing does not exist.
Question:
If dharmas are without arising, they should have abiding. Answer:
“Non-abiding dharmas do not abide; abiding dharmas also do not abide.
Even at the time of abiding, they do not abide. Since there is no arising, how could they abide?
Non-abiding dharmas do not abide because they lack the characteristic of abiding.
Dwelling itself also does not dwell. Why?
Because dwelling already exists.
Because there is going, there is staying. If the dharma of staying already existed beforehand, it would not need to stay again.
At the very time of staying, it does not stay; apart from staying and non-staying, there is no further "time of staying," and therefore it does not stay either.
Since abiding cannot be found when sought in any of these ways, it is precisely non-arising.
If there is no arising, how could there be abiding?
Furthermore:
"If all phenomena are in the process of ceasing, they should not abide;
if phenomena do not cease, such a thing [as abiding] would never exist.
If a phenomenon has the characteristic of cessation, that phenomenon lacks the characteristic of abiding.

Why is this? Because within a single dharma there are two characteristics that are mutually contradictory: the first is the characteristic of cessation, and the second is the characteristic of abiding.

For it to be the case that the characteristics of abiding and cessation exist simultaneously in one place is impossible; therefore, one cannot say that a dharma characterized by cessation possesses abiding.
Question:
If a dharma does not cease, it should abide. Answer:
There is no dharma that does not cease. Why is this?
"All dharmas whatsoever are characterized by aging and death."
"In the end, no dharma is seen that exists apart from old age and death.
When all dharmas arise, they are impermanent; this impermanence is constantly pursued by two things:
namely, old age and death.
In this way, all phenomena are constantly subject to aging and death; therefore, there is no time of abiding.
Furthermore:
"Abiding does not abide by its own characteristic, nor does it abide by a different characteristic."
Just as arising does not arise from itself, nor does it arise from other characteristics.
If there were any abiding dharma, would it abide through its own characteristic or through the characteristic of another?
Both [positions] are untenable.
If it were to abide by way of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it would be eternal.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) arise from a multitude of conditions; if a phenomenon were to abide through its own power, it could not be called "conditioned."
If abiding were to abide by its own characteristic, then dharmas would likewise have to abide by their own characteristics.
Just as the eye cannot see itself, so it is with abiding.
If abiding were to abide by a different characteristic, then that abiding would require another abiding, leading to an infinite regress.

Furthermore, one observes that distinct phenomena give rise to distinct characteristics; yet it cannot be that distinct characteristics exist without depending on distinct phenomena, for such characteristics are not fixed.
To claim that they abide by depending on these distinct characteristics is incorrect.
Question: If there is no abiding, there must be cessation. Answer:
There is none.
Why? "That which has already ceased does not cease; that which has not yet ceased also does not cease."
"When ceasing, it does not cease; if there is no arising, how can there be cessation?
If a phenomenon has already ceased, it does not cease, because it has already ceased.
That which has not yet ceased also does not cease, because it lacks the characteristic of cessation.
At the time of cessation, there is no cessation; apart from these two, there is no further time of cessation.
Investigating in this manner, the dharma of cessation is itself non-arising; if there is no arising, how can there be cessation?
Furthermore:
"If a phenomenon were to abide, it should not cease;
if a phenomenon were not to abide, it likewise should not cease."
If a dharma were fixedly established, it would not undergo cessation.
Why? Because it possesses the characteristic of abiding.
If abiding and cessation were to coexist, there would be two characteristics:
the characteristic of abiding and the characteristic of cessation.
Therefore, one cannot say that cessation exists within abiding, just as birth and death cannot exist at the same time.
If a phenomenon does not abide, it likewise has no cessation.
Why is this? Because it is devoid of the characteristic of abiding.
If one is separated from the characteristic of abiding, then there is no phenomenon;
if there is no phenomenon, how could it cease? Furthermore: "This phenomenon, at this time, does not cease at this time."
"This dharma, at another time, does not cease at a different time.
If a dharma possesses the characteristic of cessation, does that dharma cease through its own characteristic or through a different characteristic?
Both [positions] are untenable.
Why? Because, for example, milk does not perish at the very time it is milk.
Because when milk exists, the characteristic of milk remains fixed;
it does not perish even at times when it is not milk. If it were not milk, one could not say that the milk has perished.
Furthermore:
"Just as the characteristic of arising cannot be found in all phenomena, because there is no characteristic of arising, there is likewise no characteristic of cessation.

As previously investigated, since the characteristic of arising of all phenomena cannot be found, at that time there is no characteristic of cessation; for since arising is refuted, there is no arising, and how could there be cessation where there is no arising?
If your mind is still not satisfied, I shall now further explain the causes and conditions for the destruction [of things].
“If a phenomenon exists, it cannot undergo cessation;
it is impossible for a single phenomenon to possess both the characteristics of existence and non-existence.”
"When all phenomena exist, one seeks their characteristic of cessation but cannot find it.
Why is this? How can there be both existence and non-existence within a single phenomenon?"
Like light and shadow, they do not occupy the same place.
Furthermore:
"If a phenomenon is non-existent, it cannot undergo cessation."
"Just as, for example, a second head cannot be severed because it does not exist;
if a phenomenon (*dharma*) were non-existent, it would lack the characteristic of cessation. Like a second head or a third hand, it cannot be severed because it does not exist."
Furthermore:
"A phenomenon is not extinguished by its own characteristic, nor is it extinguished by another characteristic;
just as it is not produced by its own characteristic, it is not produced by another characteristic either."
As previously stated regarding the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), arising does not arise from itself, nor does it arise from another.
If it were to arise by means of its own essence, that would be impossible; rather, all things arise from a multitude of conditions (*pratyaya*).
Just as the tip of a finger cannot touch itself, so too arising cannot arise from itself.
Nor is it the case that it arises from another. Why is this?
Since arising does not yet exist, it cannot arise from another.

Because this arising is non-existent, it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); because intrinsic nature is absent, "the other" also does not exist. Therefore, arising from another is likewise untenable.
The dharma of cessation is also like this: it does not cease by its own characteristic, nor does it cease by another characteristic.
Furthermore:
"Since arising, abiding, and ceasing are not established, therefore conditioned phenomena do not exist."
"Since conditioned phenomena do not exist, how could unconditioned phenomena exist?
You previously stated that because there are the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing, conditioned phenomena exist; and because conditioned phenomena exist, unconditioned phenomena exist.
Now, when sought through reasoning, the three characteristics cannot be found; how, then, can there be conditioned phenomena?
As previously stated, there is no phenomenon that lacks characteristics; since conditioned phenomena do not exist, how could unconditioned phenomena exist?
The characteristics of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are called non-arising, non-abiding, and non-ceasing.

One names them the characteristics of the unconditioned by ceasing the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). The unconditioned itself has no distinct characteristics; it is because of these three characteristics that there are the characteristics of the unconditioned.
Just as fire has the characteristic of heat, earth has the characteristic of solidity, and water has the characteristic of coldness, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is not so.
Question:
If arising, abiding, and ceasing are ultimately non-existent, how can they be spoken of by name in the treatises?
The answer is:
"Like an illusion and like a dream, like a city of the Gandharvas—
so too are the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing that have been described."
The characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing have no fixed reality; ordinary people, out of craving and attachment, claim they do.

The noble ones, out of compassion, wish to stop such perversions, and thus they employ the very names by which others are attached to explain [the truth]. Although the words are the same, their minds are different.
Thus, when speaking of the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing, one should not raise objections.

Just as with that which is produced by illusion or transformation, one should not inquire after its origin, nor should one harbor thoughts of sorrow or joy regarding it; one should simply observe it with the eye.
Just as what is seen in a dream should not be sought as real, and just as a city of the gandharvas appears when the sun rises but has no reality, being merely a provisional name that soon perishes.
Arising, abiding, and ceasing are also like this: ordinary people discriminate them as existing, but when the wise investigate them, they cannot be found.
Chapter 8: Examination of Action and the Agent. Verse 82 asks:
Presently there is action, there is an agent, and there are the factors of action; because these three things combine, there is retribution. Therefore, there must be an agent and an action.
Answer: In the preceding chapters, all phenomena have been refuted without exception.

For example, by refuting the three characteristics, since the three characteristics do not exist, there is no conditioned phenomenon; and since conditioned phenomena do not exist, there is no unconditioned phenomenon.
Because both the conditioned and the unconditioned do not exist, all phenomena are entirely without action or an agent.
If they were conditioned, they have already been refuted within the discussion of the conditioned;
if they were unconditioned, they have already been refuted within the discussion of the unconditioned.
You should not ask further.
Because your attachment is deep, you ask again; I shall now answer once more:
"It is certain that there is an agent, yet he does not perform a determinate action."
"It is certain that there is no agent, nor does one perform indeterminate karma.
If an agent were predetermined and the action to be performed were predetermined, then it would not be something to be performed.
If it is definitively established that there is no agent and definitively established that there is no action, then one should not perform [the action].
Why is this? "Since the action is definitely non-existent as an act, this action has no agent."
"The agent is without action, and the agent is also without karma.
If the action were already definitively established prior to its performance, there would be no further need for an agent;
moreover, the action would exist independently of the agent.
However, this is not the case.
If the agent were already definitively existent prior [to action], there should be no further performance of action;
moreover, the agent would exist independently of the action.
However, this is not the case.
Therefore, there can be no action performed by a determinate agent acting upon a determinate object;
nor can there be action performed by an indeterminate agent acting upon an indeterminate object.
Why is this? Because they have been non-existent from the very beginning.
If there were a creator and a created action, one would still be unable to create; how much more so when there is neither a creator nor a created action?
Furthermore:
"If there were a determinate agent, there would also be a determinate action;
[yet] the agent and the action would both fall into the state of being causeless."

If the agent were definitively existent prior to the action and the action were definitively existent, then your claim that the agent performs the action would be without cause; for there would be an agent apart from the action and an action apart from the agent, which means they do not arise from causes and conditions.
Question:
If there were an agent and an action that existed independently of causes and conditions, what fault would there be? Answer:
"If one falls into the view of causelessness, then there would be no cause and no effect,
no action and no agent, and no phenomena to be enacted.
If such phenomena as action did not exist, then there would be neither sin nor merit."
Because sin and merit are non-existent, the retribution for sin and merit is also non-existent.
If there were no retribution for sin and merit, there would likewise be no nirvāṇa;
all things that can be produced would be empty and without fruit.
If one falls into the view of causelessness, then all phenomena would be without cause and without effect.
That which can produce is called the cause, and that which is produced is called the effect; these two would then not exist.
Because these two do not exist, there is no action, no agent, and no object of action; furthermore, there is neither sin nor merit.
Because sin and merit do not exist, there is likewise no retribution for sin and merit, nor is there the path to nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it cannot arise without a cause.
Question:
If the agent is indeterminate yet performs an indeterminate action, what fault is there?
Answer:
If even a single factor is absent, one cannot initiate an action; how much more so when both factors are entirely absent?
It is like a conjured person taking empty space for a dwelling; there is only the verbal expression, but no agent and no action.
Question:
If there were no agent and no action, nothing could be produced;
but since there is now an agent and there is an action, there must be production.
The answer is:
"Whether the agent is determinate or indeterminate, they cannot perform two actions simultaneously;
because existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory, there cannot be two in a single place."
Whether the agent is determinate or indeterminate, they cannot produce determinate or indeterminate karma.
Why? Because existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory; two [contradictory states] should not coexist in a single locus.
Existence is determinate and non-existence is indeterminate; how can existence and non-existence both apply to a single person or a single thing?
Furthermore:
"Existence cannot become non-existence, and non-existence cannot become existence."
"If there were both an agent and an action, its faults would be as previously explained.
If there is an agent but no action, how could anything be performed?
If there is no agent but there is an action, likewise nothing can be performed.
Why is this? As previously stated:
if the action already exists within existence, what further would the agent have to do?
If action did not previously exist, how could it be performed?
In that case, the causal relationship between the retribution of demerit and merit would be destroyed.

Therefore, the verse says: "That which exists cannot produce that which does not exist, and that which does not exist cannot produce that which exists; if there were a producer of what already exists, its faults would be as previously explained."
Furthermore: "An agent does not perform a determinate action, nor does he perform an indeterminate one, nor both determinate and indeterminate actions;
the faults [of such views] are as previously explained."
Fixed karma has already been refuted, as have indeterminate karma and both fixed and indeterminate karma;
now, wishing to refute them all at once, this verse is spoken: therefore, an agent cannot perform these three kinds of karma.
Now, these three kinds of agents are likewise unable to perform an action.
Why is this? "An agent is determinate, indeterminate, Or both determinate and indeterminate."
"One who cannot perform an action has faults as previously described.
Whether the agent is determinate, indeterminate, or both determinate and indeterminate, they cannot perform an action.
Why is this? It is because of the three types of faulty causes and conditions mentioned previously;
this should be explained in detail here. Thus, in all instances, when one seeks for an agent and an action, neither can be found.
Question: If one says there is no action and no agent, then one falls back into the error of causelessness. Answer:
This karma arises from a multitude of conditions; it exists only as a provisional designation and lacks any fixed determination.
It is not as you have described. Why is this so?
"Because of karma there is an agent; because of an agent there is karma.
Such is the established meaning of karma; there is nothing else besides this.
Prior to karma, there is no fixed [agent]; it is by depending on a person that karma arises.
Because of karma there is an agent, yet the agent is also not fixed.
Because of the performance of an action there is what is called an "agent"; through the conjunction of these two factors, the action and the agent are established.
If things arise from a combination of causes and conditions, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty; being empty, there is nothing that arises.
It is only in accordance with the conceptual constructions and discriminations of ordinary beings that one speaks of "action" and an "agent";
in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is neither action nor agent.
Furthermore:
"Just as the action and the agent have been refuted, so too are the sensation and the feeler;
all phenomena likewise should be refuted in this manner."

Just as the action and the agent cannot be separated from one another, because they are not separate, they are not fixed; because they are not fixed, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Feeling and the feeler are also like this:

"feeling" refers to the body of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), while the "feeler" is the person. Thus, apart from the person there are no five aggregates, and apart from the five aggregates there is no person; they arise merely from a combination of conditions, just like feeling and the feeler.
All other phenomena should likewise be refuted in this manner.
Chapter Nine: Examination of the Prior Entity. Verse 12 of the Examination of the Prior Entity asks: Some say:
“The eyes, ears, and other faculties, as well as suffering, pleasure, and other phenomena—
who possesses these things?
This is what is called the ‘pre-existent self’ (pūrvavat).”
If there were no pre-existent substrate (*pūrvaka-pudgala*), who would possess the dharmas such as the eye?
For this reason, one should know that the pre-existent substrate exists beforehand.
The various faculties, such as the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and life-force, are called the "faculties of the eye, ear," and so forth.

Painful feeling, pleasant feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, perception, volition, mindfulness, and other mental factors associated with the mind are called "dharmas such as suffering and pleasure."
A certain master of the Abhidharma says:
Prior to the existence of dharmas such as the eye, there must be a "pre-existent substrate" (*pūrvasthita*).
It is because of this pre-existent substrate that the various faculties, such as the eye, are able to develop and increase.
If there were no primordial substratum (pūrvaka), by what cause would the body and the various faculties such as the eyes arise and attain growth?
The answer is:
"If one is separated from the faculties such as the eyes, as well as from phenomena such as suffering and pleasure..."
"If there were a 'pre-existent dweller' prior [to the faculties], by what could it be known?
If there were a pre-existent dweller prior to the sense organs such as the eyes and ears, or to phenomena such as suffering and pleasure, by what means could it be described?
How can this be known?
Just as external phenomena such as jars and garments are known through the sense organs of the eye and so forth,
internal phenomena are known through the faculties of sensation, such as suffering and pleasure.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"That which is subject to disintegration is the characteristic of form; that which is capable of feeling is the characteristic of sensation; that which is capable of cognizing is the characteristic of consciousness.
You claim that there exists a "pre-existing dweller" prior to the eyes, ears, suffering, pleasure, and so forth; by what means can this be known, such that you assert the existence of such a dharma?
Question: Some masters of the treatises say that inhalation and exhalation,
looking and blinking, life-span, volition, suffering and pleasure, hatred and love, and movement and initiation are the characteristics of the self (ātman).
If there were no self (ātman), how could there be such phenomena as inhalation and exhalation?
Therefore, one should know that prior to the sense organs such as the eyes and ears, and prior to dharmas such as suffering and pleasure, there exists a primordial abider (pūrvasthita).
The answer is:
If this self (ātman) exists, it must be within the body, like a pillar within a wall;
or it must be outside the body, like a person wearing armor.
If the spirit were within the body, the body would be indestructible, because the spirit would always reside within it.
Therefore, to say that the spirit is within the body is merely a verbal assertion; it is empty, false, and without reality.
If it were outside the body and covered the body like armor, the body should be invisible, because it would be covered by something subtle and dense;
furthermore, it should be indestructible, yet in reality we see the body perish.
Therefore, one should know that apart from suffering, pleasure, and so forth, there is no other dharma existing prior to them.

If it is claimed that when an arm is severed, the *ātman* contracts and remains within so that it cannot be severed, then when the head is severed, it should likewise contract and remain within and thus not die; yet, in reality, death occurs.
Therefore, one should know that the claim that there exists a self (ātman) prior to and apart from suffering, pleasure, and so forth, is merely a verbal assertion; it is false and devoid of reality.

Furthermore, if one says that the self is large when the body is large and small when the body is small—just as light is large when a lamp is large and small when a lamp is small—then such a self would not be permanent, as it would necessarily follow the body.
If it were to follow the body, then where there is no body, there would be no spirit, just as when a lamp is extinguished, its light is extinguished.
If the spirit were impermanent, it would be identical to the eyes, ears, suffering, and pleasure.
Therefore, one should know that apart from the eye, ear, and so forth, there is no separate self (*ātman*) existing prior to them.
Furthermore, just as a person suffering from wind-disorder (*vāta-roga*) loses their autonomy and acts in ways they ought not to act; so it is with the self.
If there were a deity who is the master of all actions, how could one say that [the self] lacks sovereignty?
If the affliction of insanity did not disturb the deity, then it would follow that there must be something distinct from the deity that performs the action.

Through such various investigations, one finds that apart from the sense organs such as the eyes and ears, and apart from phenomena such as suffering and pleasure, there is no pre-existing person (*pudgala*).

If one were to insist that there exists a pre-existing person apart from the sense organs such as the eyes and ears and apart from phenomena such as suffering and pleasure, such a thing is impossible.
Why is this? "If there were a 'pre-existent self' apart from the eyes, ears, and so forth;
then there should likewise be eyes, ears, and so forth, apart from that pre-existent self."

If the primordial substrate existed prior to and independent of the faculties such as the eyes and ears, as well as phenomena such as suffering and pleasure, then now the faculties such as the eyes and ears, and phenomena such as suffering and pleasure, should likewise exist independently of the primordial substrate.
Question:
It may be that these two things are separate, provided only that there exists a "resident self" (āśraya). Answer:
"By means of dharmas one knows there is a person; by means of a person one knows there are dharmas.
Apart from dharmas, how could there be a person?
Apart from a person, how could there be dharmas?"
"Phenomena" (dharma) refer to the eye, ear, suffering, pleasure, and so forth.
"Person" (pudgala) refers to the primordial substrate (pūrvavat).
You claim that because phenomena exist, one knows there is a person; and because a person exists, one knows there are phenomena.
Now, apart from the dharmas such as the eye and the ear, what person exists?
And apart from the person, what dharmas such as the eye and the ear exist?
Furthermore:
"In all faculties such as the eye, there is in reality no underlying substratum (*pudgala*);
the various faculties such as the eye and ear are distinguished by their differing characteristics.
In the various faculties such as the eye and ear, and in all phenomena such as suffering and pleasure, there is in reality no underlying substratum.

Visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and forms; it is through these combined causes and conditions that one knows the existence of the various faculties such as the eye and ear, rather than knowing them by means of a "resident self" (pudgala).
Therefore, the verse states: "All faculties, such as the eye, truly have no resident self"; the various faculties, such as the eye and ear, are each capable of their own discernment.
Question:
"If there is no 'resident self' (pudgala) for the various faculties such as the eye,
how can each individual faculty, such as the eye, perceive its respective object?"

"If all the sense faculties, such as the eyes and ears, and all phenomena, such as suffering and pleasure, lacked a fundamental abiding entity (*pūrvasthita*), how could each individual faculty now perceive its respective object?"
The various faculties, such as the eye and ear, lack volitional thought and thus should not possess cognition;
yet they actually cognize objects. One should therefore know that apart from the eye, ear, and other faculties, there exists another agent capable of cognizing objects.
Answer: If that were so,
would there be a distinct knower within each individual sense organ,
or would there be a single knower residing within all the sense organs?
Both positions entail faults. Why is this?
"The seer is the hearer; the hearer is the feeler."
If these various faculties were thus, there would necessarily be a pre-existent self.
If the seer were the hearer, and the hearer were the feeler, then there would be a single soul.
In this way, the various faculties such as the eye would have to exist prior to their objects;

yet, regarding forms, sounds, odors, and so forth, there is no fixed knower, for one might possibly hear a sound with the eye, just as a person who possesses six directions perceives and hears according to whichever direction they face.
If the hearer and the seer were one and the same, then hearing and seeing would follow the respective faculties of the eye and so forth;
however, this is not the case. "If the seer and the hearer are distinct, The experiencer must also be distinct.
At the time of seeing, one should also hear; In that case, the self (ātman) would be manifold."
If the seer, the hearer, and the feeler were each distinct, then at the time of seeing, one should also hear.
Why? Because there would be a hearer existing apart from the seer.
In this way, within the nose, tongue, and body, the spirit (*ātman*) should function simultaneously.
If that were so, there would be one person with many spirits, as all the sense-faculties would cognize their respective objects at once.
But in reality this is not so; therefore, the seer, the hearer, and the feeler should not be employed simultaneously.
Furthermore:
"The various faculties, such as the eye and ear, And the various phenomena, such as suffering and pleasure..."
"The great elements from which [the body] arises—those elements likewise have no self.
Thus, the claim that there exists a "substratum" (pudgala) distinct from the sense organs such as the eyes and ears, or from phenomena such as suffering and pleasure, has already been refuted.
Now, regarding the four great elements that serve as the causes for the eyes, ears, and so forth, within these four great elements there is likewise no primordial dweller (*puruṣa*).
Question:
It may be granted that there is no primordial dweller in the various faculties such as the eyes and ears, or in the various phenomena such as suffering and pleasure.
The various faculties such as the eye and ear, and the various phenomena such as suffering and pleasure, ought to exist.
The answer says:
"If the faculties such as the eye and ear, and the various phenomena such as suffering and pleasure..."
"If there were no primary self (pudgala), then the eyes and so forth would also not exist.
If the dharmas such as the eyes, ears, suffering, and pleasure have no primary self, who possesses these eyes, ears, and so forth?
By what cause would they exist?
Therefore, the eye, ear, and so forth are likewise non-existent.
Furthermore:
"The eye and so forth have no prior abider; they likewise do not exist now or hereafter.
Because they do not exist in the three times, there is no non-discrimination.
When one contemplates and investigates a prior abider, it does not exist prior to the eye and so forth, nor does it exist now or hereafter.
If the three times do not exist, this is precisely non-arising and quiescence.
One should not raise the objection:
"If there is no primordial abiding, how can there be the eye and so forth?"
Through such question and answer, conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is extinguished.
Because conceptual proliferation is extinguished, all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty.
Chapter 10: Examination of Fire and Fuel. Verse 16 of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, Chapter Ten: Examination of Fire and Fuel. Question:
"There must be sensation and a feeler, just as there is fire and fuel; fire is the feeler and fuel is the sensation, namely the five aggregates.
The answer is: "This is not so."
Why is this? Because both the fire and the fuel are unestablished.
Whether the fire and the fuel are established by means of a single dharma or by means of two dharmas, in either case they are unestablished.
Question: Setting aside for a moment the doctrine of identity and difference,
if one says there is neither fire nor fuel, how can one now refute [the opponent] by means of the characteristics of identity and difference?
Just as the horns of a rabbit or the hair of a tortoise cannot be refuted because they do not exist,
so too must one first perceive a real thing with the eyes of the world before it can be subject to reflection;
just as only when gold exists can it be burned or forged.
If there were neither fire nor fuel, one should not contemplate them through the categories of identity or difference.
If you admit the categories of identity or difference, you should know that fire and fuel exist.
If one allows that it exists, then it must already exist.
The answer is:
according to conventional worldly discourse, there should be no fault.
Whether one asserts that the fuel and the combustible are identical or distinct, it cannot be called "acceptance.
If one were to depart from conventional discourse, there would be nothing to discuss.
If one does not speak of fuel and the combustible, how could there be anything to refute?
If there were nothing spoken, then the meaning could not be clarified.

For instance, if a proponent wishes to refute existence and non-existence, they must necessarily speak of existence and non-existence; it is not because they utter the terms "existence" and "non-existence" that they thereby accept existence and non-existence.
Therefore, there is no fault because one conforms to worldly conventions of speech.
If having words in the mouth were itself to constitute being a recipient, then your statement that "it is destroyed" would mean you yourself are destroyed; the same applies to fire and fuel.

Although there are such verbal expressions, they are not accepted as ultimate reality; therefore, when one contemplates the fire and the fuel through the categories of identity or difference, neither is established. Why is this so?
"If the fire were the fuel, then the agent and the action would be one;
if the fire were different from the fuel, then there would be fire apart from the fuel.
Here, "fire" refers to the flame, and "fuel" refers to the wood.
The agent is a person, and this is the action.
If the fire and the fuel were one, then the action and the agent would also have to be one.
If the action and the agent were one, then the potter and the jar would be one.
The maker is the potter and the made is the jar; yet the potter is not the jar, and the jar is not the potter. How, then, could they be one?
Therefore, the action and the agent are not one;
likewise, the fuel and the burner are also not one.
If it is argued that since unity is impossible,
there must be difference, this too is not correct. Why is that?
If fire were different from the fuel, there would have to be fire existing separately, apart from the fuel.
One could distinguish "this is the fuel" and "this is the fire," and in every case, there would have to be fire apart from the fuel.
But in reality this is not so; therefore, difference is also untenable.
Furthermore:
"In that case, [fire] would always be burning, / Not arising in dependence upon the fuel."
"Then there would be no function of kindling fire, and it would also be called 'unconditioned fire.
If the fire and the fuel were different, then the fire would not depend on the fuel and would burn eternally."
If it were burning constantly, it would abide in its own essence independently of causes and conditions, and human effort would be in vain.
Human effort consists of protecting the fire so that it continues to burn.
This function exists; therefore, one knows that fire is not different from the fuel.
Furthermore, if fire were different from the fuel, fire would be without action.
Apart from the fuel, what would fire burn?
If that were so, fire would be without action.
There is no such thing as fire without action.
Question:
"How is it that fire does not arise from causes and conditions, and human effort is likewise empty?
He replied:
"If burning does not depend on what is to be burned, then it does not arise from conditions."
"If fire were to burn eternally, human effort would be rendered useless.
If the burning agent and the combustible object were distinct, then there would be a burning agent that does not depend upon the combustible object.
If combustion were to exist without depending on the combustible, then there would be no phenomena characterized by mutual causality; therefore, it would not arise from causes and conditions.
Furthermore, if combustion were distinct from the combustible, it would follow that it burns eternally.
If fire were always burning, it would be perceived as existing separately from the fuel, and no further human effort would be required. Why?
"If you claim that when it is burning, it is called 'fuel';"
At that time, there would be only fuel; what thing could then be the "combustible" that burns?
If you claim that fuel exists beforehand and is called the "combustible" at the time of burning, this is not so.
If the fuel existed separately from the fire, how could one say that what is burning at that time is called "fuel"?
Furthermore:
"If they were different, they would not meet; if they do not meet, there is no burning."
"If it does not burn, it does not cease; if it does not cease, it abides eternally.
If the fire were different from the fuel, then the fire would not reach the fuel. Why is this so?
Because they are established without depending on one another.
If fire were established without depending on the fuel, it would abide in its own essence; what need would it have for fuel?
Therefore, there is no reaching.
If [fire] does not reach [the fuel], then it does not burn the fuel. Why?
Because there is no such thing as burning that which has not been reached.
If it were not burned, there would be no cessation, and it should therefore abide eternally in its own characteristic.
But this is not the case. Question:
"If the fire were different from the fuel, it could reach the fuel;
likewise, that person could reach this person, and this person could reach that person.
If the fire were different from the fuel, it could reach the fuel.
As it is for a man approaching a woman, so it is for a woman approaching a man.
He replied:
"If one says that fire and the fuel are both mutually separate,"
"If it burns in this way, it can reach that which is to be burned.
If there were fuel apart from the fire, or if there were fire apart from the fuel, such that each existed independently, then in that case the fire would indeed reach the fuel.
But in reality, this is not so.
Why? Because there is no fuel apart from fire, and there is no fire apart from fuel.
Now, since there is a woman apart from a man, and a man apart from a woman, your analogy is therefore incorrect.
Because the analogy is not established, fire does not reach the fuel.
[The opponent] asks:

Fire and the fuel for burning exist in mutual dependence; fire exists because of the fuel, and the fuel exists because of the fire. These two phenomena are established through their mutual dependence.
The answer says:
"If fire depends on fuel, and fuel exists because of fire..."
First, one must determine what dharma exists such that there is both fuel and that which burns.
If fire is established because of fuel, then fuel must likewise be established because of fire.
In this regard, if the fuel were definitively existent prior [to the fire], then the fire would be established by depending on that fuel.
If the fire were definitively existent prior [to the fuel], then the fuel would be established by depending on that fire.
Now, if fire were to be established by depending on fuel, then fuel would exist first and fire would exist later; it should not be the case that fuel exists only by depending on fire. Why is this so?
Because the combustible exists first and the burning exists later.
If the burning does not burn the combustible, then the combustible is not established;
furthermore, the combustible does not exist elsewhere, as it is distinct from the burning.
If the fuel is not established, the fire is also not established.
If the fire were to exist first and the fuel were to follow later, the fire would likewise incur this same fault.
Therefore, both fire and fuel are unestablished.
Furthermore:
"If fire were to exist because of fuel, then fire would be established and yet established again;
this means that within the fuel, there would be no fire."
If one intends for fire to be established by means of fuel, then once the fire is established, it would be established yet again. Why?
Because the fire would abide within itself.
If fire, not abiding in its own essence, were to be produced from fuel, such a thing would be impossible.
Therefore, if there were such a fire produced from fuel, then that which is already established would be established once again; thus, there would be this logical fallacy.
Furthermore, there is the fault that the fuel would exist without the fire. Why?
Because the fuel would abide in its own essence, independent of the fire.
Therefore, it is impossible for fire and fuel to exist as mutually dependent.
Furthermore:
"If a phenomenon is established through dependence, that very phenomenon is itself dependent."
"Now there is no dependence on causes, nor is there any dharma that is established.
If a dharma were established through dependence on causes, that dharma would in turn become the very cause upon which it depends.
In such a case, there would definitively be no two distinct things.
Just as fire is established by means of fuel, and fuel is established by means of fire, both are thus indeterminate.
Because they are indeterminate, they cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? "If a phenomenon is established in dependence, how can it depend when it is not yet established?
If it is already established and then depends, what use is there for dependence once it is established?"

If a phenomenon is established through dependence, that phenomenon did not exist prior to its establishment; since it was unestablished, it did not exist, and if it does not exist, how can there be dependence?
If a phenomenon were already established prior to this, what need would there be for dependence once it is already established?
These two are not mutually dependent; therefore, your previous assertion that fire and fuel are established through mutual dependence is untenable.
Thus: "Without fuel there is no fire; Even without [fuel] as a cause, there is no fire."
"Without fuel, there is no fire; without depending on fuel, fire does not exist.
Now, fire is not established by depending on fuel, nor is fire established without depending on fuel.
The combustible is also like this.
Whether it depends on the fire or does not depend on the fire, both positions are untenable; these faults have already been explained previously.
Furthermore:
"Fire does not come from elsewhere; fire is also not present where it burns.
Fuel is likewise so; the rest is as explained in the discussion on 'going' and 'coming'.
Fire does not enter the fuel from another direction, nor is fire present within the fuel, because fire cannot be found when one seeks it by analyzing the wood.
The fuel is also like this: it does not come from elsewhere to enter into the fire, nor is there fuel within the fire.

Just as that which has already burned does not burn, that which has not yet burned does not burn, and that which is currently burning does not burn—this principle is as explained in the [chapter on] "Going and Coming."
Therefore: "The fuel is not the burning; apart from the fuel there is no burning.
There is no burning without fuel; within the burning there is no fuel."
"There is no burning within the fuel;
the fuel itself is not the burning. Why is this?"
This has already been explained previously through the fault of the identity of action and agent.
Furthermore, apart from the fuel there would be no fire, which would entail the faults of fire being eternal and so forth.

Fire does not exist within the fuel, fire does not exist in the fire itself, and the fuel does not exist within the fire; because these would entail the fault of difference (*anyatva*), all three positions are untenable.
Question:
For what reason are the fire and the fuel spoken of? Answer:
Just as there is fire because of combustible fuel, so there is an experiencer because of sensation (*vedanā*).
"Sensation" refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), and the "experiencer" refers to the person (*pudgala*).
Since fire and combustible fuel are not established [as independent entities], sensation and the experiencer are likewise not established.
Why is this? "By means of the principles of fire and fuel, one explains the principles of the experiencer and the experienced,
as well as the jar, the garment, and all other such phenomena."
"Just as the fuel is not the fire, so too the sensation is not the feeler, because it would entail the error of identity between the action and the agent.
Furthermore, there is no feeler apart from the sensation, for they cannot be found to be distinct."
Because of these distinct fallacies, all three [positions] are untenable.

Just as with the analysis of sensation and the feeler, so it is for all external phenomena such as jars, garments, and so forth; they are all explained above as being without arising and ultimately empty.
Therefore: "If a person asserts a self, And that all phenomena have distinct characteristics;
Know that such a person Shall not obtain the flavor of the Buddha-dharma."
All dharmas are, from their very origin, unarisen and possess the characteristic of ultimate quiescence; for this reason, at the end of this chapter, these verses are spoken.

If one speaks of the mark of a self (*ātman*), as the Vātsīputrīyas do—claiming that one cannot say "form is the self," nor can one say "the self is apart from form," because the self exists within the fifth, inexpressible category (*avaktavya-skandha*)—[this is refuted by the following].
As the Sarvāstivāda school explains:
the individual characteristics of all phenomena are distinguished as being wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate;
as being with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava); and as being conditioned (saṃskṛta) or unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and so forth.
Such persons do not attain the mark of the quiescence of all phenomena, yet they engage in various conceptual proliferations based on the Buddha’s words.
Chapter Eleven: Examination of the Beginning. In the eleventh chapter, "Examination of the Beginning," there are eight verses.
Question: The *Anavarāgra-sūtra* states:
Sentient beings come and go within birth and death, yet their original limit (pūrvakoṭi) cannot be apprehended.
Within this, it is said that there are sentient beings and there is birth and death.
For what reason and by what causal conditions is this taught?
The answer was:
"That which is taught by the Great Sage: the ultimate limit (pūrvakoṭi) cannot be found;
birth and death have no beginning, nor do they have an end."
"There are three kinds of noble ones:
first, those non-Buddhists who possess the five supernormal powers;
second, arhats and pratyekabuddhas."
Third, there are great bodhisattvas who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Among these three types, the Buddha is the most supreme; therefore, he is called the Great Sage (*mahāmuni*).
Whatever the Buddha speaks is nothing other than the utterance of truth.
Birth and death have no beginning. Why is this?
Because a beginning or an end to birth and death cannot be apprehended; therefore, it is said to be without beginning.
If you claim that if there is neither beginning nor end, there must be a middle, this too is not so.
Why? "If there is no beginning or end, how could there be a middle?"
"Therefore, within this, neither the prior, the subsequent, nor both together exist.
For there is the beginning because of the middle and the end; there is the end because of the beginning and the middle.
If there is neither beginning nor end, how can there be a middle?
Within birth and death, there is no beginning, middle, or end; therefore, it is said that the prior, the posterior, and their combination cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? "If birth were to exist first, and old age and death later;
then there would be birth without old age and death, and there would be old age and death without birth."
If old age and death existed first, and birth existed afterward, then [birth] would be without cause; there would be no old age and death for that which has not been born.
If, among living beings in the cycle of birth and death, birth occurred first and then gradually followed old age and subsequently death, then birth would be devoid of old age and death.
According to the nature of phenomena, there must be birth for there to be aging and death, and aging and death for there to be birth.
Furthermore, it is not the case that one is born without aging and death;
nor is it the case that aging and death exist without being caused by birth.
If old age and death were to occur first and birth later, then old age and death would be without a cause, because birth would come after them;
furthermore, if there is no birth, how could there be old age and death?
If one claims that it is impossible for birth and old age and death to be sequential, and asserts that they are established simultaneously, this too is flawed.
Why is this? "Birth and old age-and-death cannot coexist at one time;
if death existed at the time of birth, both would be without cause."
If birth, old age, and death were simultaneous, it would not be so. Why?
Because death would exist at the very moment of birth.
According to the nature of phenomena, they should exist at the time of birth and not exist at the time of death; yet if there were death while one is being born, this would be impossible.
If birth and death occurred simultaneously, then there could be no mutual causality between them.
Just as the horns of an ox emerge simultaneously and thus do not depend upon one another,
it is said:
"If the beginning and the end were to exist together, none of these would be tenable."
"For what reason do you engage in conceptual proliferation, claiming that there is birth, aging, and death?
By contemplating that birth, aging, and death all possess faults, one realizes that there is no birth; they are ultimately empty.
Why do you now cling to conceptual proliferation regarding birth, aging, and death, asserting that they possess a determinate nature?
Furthermore:
"All causes and effects, as well as characteristics and the phenomena characterized by them..."
Feelings, the feeler, and so forth— all phenomena whatsoever—
are not found at the beginning of saṃsāra alone;
likewise, all such phenomena are likewise non-existent at their original limit.

"All dharmas" refers to causes and effects, the characterized and the characteristics, sensation and the feeler, and so forth; all of these lack a fundamental limit (*anavarāgra*), not only is birth and death without a fundamental limit.
Because it is taught by way of a brief exposition, it is said that there is no beginning to birth and death.
Chapter 12: Examination of Suffering (Duḥkha-parīkṣā), the Tenth Chapter of the Treatise, consisting of twenty verses. Some say:
"Whether created by oneself, created by another, created by both, or produced without cause,"
Thus it is said regarding all sufferings, yet this is not the case with respect to their fruit.
Some say that suffering and affliction are self-created;
Some say it is created by another;
some say it is both self-created and created by another;
others say it arises without cause—none of these apply to the fruit.
Regarding the statement that "in the case of the fruit, none are so": sentient beings undergo suffering due to various conditions; weary of suffering, they desire its cessation.
Yet, being unaware of the true causes and conditions of their affliction, they fall into four kinds of errors. For this reason, it is said that "in the case of the fruit, none are so."
Why is this? "If suffering were self-made, it would not arise from conditions;
rather, because these aggregates exist, those aggregates arise."
If suffering were self-made, it would not arise from a multitude of conditions; "self-made" would mean arising from its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This is not the case. Why?
Because the subsequent five aggregates arise due to the preceding five aggregates, suffering cannot be self-created.
Question: If one says that these five aggregates create those five aggregates, then it would be created by another.
Answer: This is not so. Why is that?
"If one says that these five aggregates are different from those five aggregates,
then it must be said that suffering is produced by another.
If these five aggregates were different from those five aggregates, and those five aggregates were different from these five aggregates, then [suffering] would have to be produced by another.
If the thread were different from the cloth, the cloth would have to exist apart from the thread.
If there is no cloth apart from the thread, then the cloth is not different from the thread.
Likewise, if those five aggregates were different from these five aggregates, then those five aggregates would have to exist apart from these five aggregates.

If those five aggregates did not exist apart from these five aggregates, then these five aggregates would not be different from those five aggregates; therefore, one should not say that suffering is produced by another.
Question: Regarding "self-agency," it means that this person creates suffering for themselves and experiences suffering for themselves. Answer:
"If a person creates suffering for themselves, apart from suffering,
what person is there who could create suffering for that very person? If one claims that a person creates their own suffering,
then apart from the suffering of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), where else is there a distinct person who could create suffering?
One should say that this person [is the one who experiences suffering], yet it cannot be said [that they are its creator];

therefore, suffering is not created by the person themselves. If it is claimed that the person does not create their own suffering, but another creates suffering and gives it to this person, that too is not correct.
Why is this? "If suffering were created by another and bestowed upon this person,
then when one is separated from that suffering, how could there be this person who receives it?"
If another person were to create suffering and give it to this individual, there would be no such recipient existing apart from the five aggregates.
Furthermore:
"If suffering were created by that other person and brought to this individual..."
"Apart from suffering, what person could there be who is able to bestow this?

If one were to say that a certain person creates suffering and bestows it upon another, then apart from the suffering of the five aggregates, what such person could there be who creates suffering and holds it to give to this other?
If it exists, its characteristics should be explained.
Furthermore:
"If that which is self-made is not established, how can suffering be made by another?"
"If that person were to create suffering, it would likewise be called 'self-created.
Since suffering cannot be self-created through any such causes and conditions, yet you claim that suffering is created by another."
This is also not the case.
Why? Because this and that exist in mutual dependence.
If that [other] were to produce suffering, it would likewise be called "self-made" suffering for that [self].
Since the notion of self-made suffering has already been refuted and your acceptance of self-made suffering is untenable, the notion of other-made [suffering] is also untenable.
Furthermore:
"Suffering is not called self-made; phenomena do not produce themselves.
Since they lack intrinsic nature, how could there be a maker of suffering?"
"It is not the case that suffering is created by oneself. Why?
Because it is like a sword that cannot cut itself."
In this way, a phenomenon cannot produce itself; therefore, it cannot be self-created.
Nor is it created by another. Why is this so?
Apart from suffering, that self-nature does not exist.
If that self-nature existed apart from suffering, one would have to say that it creates suffering; yet it is itself suffering—how, then, could suffering create suffering for itself?
Question:
If it is not the case that [suffering] is created by oneself or created by another, then it must be created by both. Answer:
"If this [self] and that [other] were to produce suffering, there would have to be suffering produced by both together;
yet since even 'this' and 'that' do not act as agents, how much more so for something produced without a cause!
Since there are faults in both self-production and production by another, how much more so for production without a cause!
There are many fallacies regarding the absence of causes, as explained in the "Chapter on Refuting the Act and the Agent.
Furthermore:
"Not only is it said that suffering [is unproduced], but the fourfold meaning is also not established."
"All external myriad things, the four meanings are likewise not established.

Although within the Buddha-dharma it is taught that the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) are suffering, there are non-Buddhist practitioners who claim that only painful sensation (*duḥkhā-vedanā*) is suffering; therefore, it is said that not only do the four meanings of "suffering" fail to be established, but all external myriad things—earth, water, mountains, trees, and so forth—all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*), are likewise not established.
Chapter Thirteen: On Contemplative Practice (Pratipatti-pariccheda) Question:
As stated in the Buddha’s sūtras, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are deceptive because they are grasped through false conceptualization;
it is for this reason that they are called "deceptive. *Note: This is verse 1 of Chapter 13.*
In the Buddha’s sūtras it is said that what is deceptive is the grasping of false signs;
the ultimate reality is nirvāṇa, which is not the grasping of false signs.
Because this sūtra says so, one should know that there are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) characterized by falsity, deception, and false grasping.
The answer is:
"Regarding 'falsity, deception, and false grasping,' what is it therein that is grasped?"
"The Buddha spoke of these matters in order to demonstrate the meaning of emptiness.
If dharmas that grasp at signs falsely are indeed deceptive, then among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), what is there to be grasped?
The Buddha has spoken thus; one should know that he was speaking of the meaning of emptiness.
Question: How is it known that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are empty?
Answer: All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are empty because they are characterized by falsity.
Conditioned phenomena are empty because they arise and perish without abiding, and because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are called the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), because they arise from conditioning.
The five aggregates are called "conditioned" because these five aggregates are all false and devoid of any fixed characteristic. Why is this so?

Just as the form of infancy is not the form of crawling, the form of crawling is not the form of walking, the form of walking is not the form of childhood, the form of childhood is not the form of youth, and the form of youth is not the form of old age.
Just as form does not abide from moment to moment, a determinate nature cannot be found through conceptualization.
Is the form of an infant identical to the form of a crawling child, and so on, up to the form of an old person, or is it different? Both positions entail logical fallacies.

Why is this? If the color-form of an infant were identical to the color-form of crawling, and so on up to the color-form of old age, then in that case all color-form would be merely that of an infant, and there would be no such thing as crawling or even old age.
Furthermore, just as a lump of clay is always a lump of clay and never becomes a jar,
why is this? Because its form (rūpa) is eternally fixed.
If the color of an infant were different from the color of one crawling on hands and knees, then the infant would not become a crawler, nor would the crawler become an infant. Why?
Because the two colors are different.
In this way, the physical forms of childhood, youth, middle age, and old age should not exist in succession; the laws of kinship would be lost, and there would be neither father nor son.
If that were so, only the infant would be entitled to have a father, while all others—from crawling infants up to the elderly—would have no such share.
Therefore, both positions are flawed. Question:
Although form is not fixed, once the form of an infant has ceased, it arises again in a continuous succession until the form of old age; thus, there is no fault as described above.
Answer: Regarding the continuous arising of the infant’s form, does it arise as a continuity after having ceased,
or does it arise as a continuity without having ceased?
If the form of an infant were to cease, how could there be a continuity?
Because there would be no cause.
It is like when there is fuel that can be burned, yet because the fire has been extinguished, there is no continuity.
If the form of an infant were not to cease but were to continue, then that infant’s form would not cease; it would remain eternally in its original state, and there would likewise be no continuity.

Question: I do not say that continuity arises because of ceasing or not ceasing; rather, I say that continuity arises because of the arising of something similar that does not abide. Therefore, I speak of "arising as continuity."
Answer: If that were so, then there would be fixed forms that are produced anew, and thus there would have to be thousands of millions of kinds of forms.
However, this is not the case; likewise, there is no continuity.
In this way, when one seeks form in all places, no fixed characteristic is found; it exists only by way of conventional designation.
