If one understands in this way, what benefit is there? Answer:
If a practitioner of the Path can penetrate such meanings, they will realize that all phenomena are neither identical nor different, neither annihilated nor eternal.

If one can do so, they will extinguish all afflictions and conceptual proliferation, attaining the eternal bliss of Nirvana; therefore, it is said that the Buddhas teach and transform beings with the flavor of ambrosia.

Just as it is said in the world that one who attains the celestial ambrosial nectar (amṛta) is free from old age, sickness, death, and all forms of decay and affliction, so too this Dharma of the true mark (lakṣaṇa) is the true flavor of ambrosia. The Buddha taught that there are three kinds of the true mark:
if one attains the true mark of all phenomena and extinguishes all afflictions (kleśa), it is called the Śrāvaka-dharma;
If one gives rise to great compassion and resolves upon the unsurpassed mind, it is called the Mahāyāna;
if no Buddha has appeared in the world and there is no Buddha-dharma, the pratyekabuddha produces wisdom through seclusion.

If a Buddha has already delivered sentient beings and entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, such that the remaining Dharma has been extinguished, those from previous lives who were destined to attain the Way may, through a slight contemplation of the causes and conditions for wearying detachment, enter the mountain forests alone to distance themselves from clamor and attain the Way; these are called *pratyekabuddhas*.
Chapter 19: An Analysis of Time (Kāla-parīkṣā) Six verses. Question:
Time must exist, because it is established through dependence upon causes.
Because there is past time, there are future and present times.
Because of the present time, there are the past and future times;
because of the future time, there are the past and present times.
Phenomena such as superior, middling, and inferior, or one and many, likewise exist through mutual dependence.
The answer is:
"If the future and the present exist because of the past time,
then the future and the present should be located within the past time."
If the future and present times existed because of the past time, then the future and present times would have to exist within the past time.
Why is this? Because wherever there is a cause for a phenomenon to be established, that phenomenon must exist in that place.
For example, as light is established in dependence upon a lamp, wherever there is a lamp, there must be light.
If, by means of the past time, the future and present times were established, then the future and present times would have to exist within the past time.
If the future and present times were contained within the past time, then all three times would be designated as the past time. Why?
Because the future and present times would exist within the past time.
If all time were entirely past, then there would be no future or present time, because everything would have already passed away.
If there were no future or present time, there should likewise be no past time.
Why is this? Because the past time is designated as "past" by reason of the future and present times.
Just as the future and present times are established by reason of the past time, so too should the past time be established by reason of the future and present times.
Since future and present time do not exist now, past time should likewise not exist.
Therefore, what was previously stated—that future and present time are established by means of past time—is incorrect.
If it is claimed that within the past time there is no future or present time, yet the future and present times are established by means of the past time— this is not so.
Why is this? "If, within the time of the past, there were no future or present;
how could the future and present depend upon the past?"
If the future and present times do not exist within the past time, how can the future and present times be established by means of the past time?

Why is this? If the three times possessed distinct characteristics, they could not be established through mutual dependence, just as objects such as jars and garments are each established independently without depending on one another.
Now, if the past time does not exist, then the future and present times cannot be established.
If the present time does not exist, then the past and future times cannot be established.
If the future time does not exist, then the past and present times cannot be established.

As for your previous statement that, although the future and present times do not exist within the past time, the future and present times are nevertheless established by means of the past time—[this is untenable].
This is not the case.
[The opponent] asks:
If future and present time are not established by depending on past time, what fault is there?
The answer is:
"Without depending on the past time, there is no future time, nor is there a present time; therefore, there are no two times."
Without depending on past time, future and present time are not established. Why is this?
If present time did not depend upon past time, in what location would present time exist?
The future is likewise; in what location does the future time exist?
Therefore, without depending on past time, there is no future or present time. Since they exist only through such mutual dependence, in reality, time does not exist.
"By virtue of this principle, one should know that in the other two times [the past and present],
the categories of superior, middling, and inferior, as well as identity and difference— such phenomena as these all do not exist. By virtue of this principle,

one should know that the remaining [times], namely the future and the present, should likewise be non-existent, and that all such phenomena as the superior, middling, and inferior, or identity and difference, should also all be non-existent.
Just as there are superior, middling, and inferior [levels] based on the superior, if one were separated from the superior, then the middling and inferior would not exist.
If the middling and inferior existed apart from the superior, they should not be mutually dependent.
Because of the one, there is the other; because of the other, there is the one. If the one truly exists, it should not exist by depending on the other.
If it were something distinct from the real entity, it should not exist by virtue of that one [entity].
All such phenomena should likewise be refuted in this manner.
Question:
Just as there are distinctions such as years, months, days, and moments, we know that time exists.
The answer says:
"The abiding of time cannot be apprehended, nor can the passing of time be apprehended."
If time cannot be apprehended, how can one speak of the characteristics of time?
Time exists because of things; apart from things, how could there be time?
Since even things do not exist, how much less could there be time!
If time does not abide, it cannot be apprehended; yet time abiding also does not exist.
If time cannot be apprehended, how can one speak of the characteristics of time?
If there are no characteristics of time, then time does not exist.
Because time arises dependent upon things, it is called "time"; if one is separated from things, there is no time.
Having refuted all things through various causes and conditions above, since things do not exist, how can there be time?
Chapter 20: Examination of Cause and Effect. Verse 24. Question:
Since an effect is observed to arise from the conjunction of various causes and conditions, one should know that this effect exists by virtue of the conjunction of those various conditions.
The answer is:
"If a fruit arises when various conditions are in harmony, it must already exist within that harmony;
why then would it need to be produced by the harmony?"
If it is claimed that when various causes and conditions combine, a fruit arises, and that this fruit already exists within the combination itself,
yet arises from that combination— this is not the case.
Why is this? If the fruit already possessed a fixed essence prior to its arising, it should not be produced from a combination of conditions.
Question:
If there is no fruit within the combination of various conditions, yet the fruit arises from those various conditions, what fault is there?
The answer is:
"If, within the combination of various conditions, there is no fruit therein..."
"How is it that from a collection of conditions, a fruit arises through their conjunction?
If a fruit arises from the conjunction of conditions, then the fruit does not exist within that conjunction, yet it arises from that conjunction.
This is not so. Why? Because if a thing lacks intrinsic nature, that thing will never arise.
Furthermore:
"If, when the various conditions are assembled, there were a fruit within them;
it would have to exist within that assembly, yet in reality it cannot be found."

If a fruit were to exist within the combination of various conditions, then that which is material (rūpa) should be visible to the eye, and that which is non-material (arūpa) should be cognizable by the mind; yet, in reality, no fruit can be found within the combination.
Therefore, it is not the case that the effect exists within the collection [of conditions].
Furthermore:
"If, when the various conditions are assembled, there is no effect therein;"
"Then these manifold causes and conditions would be identical to non-causes and non-conditions.
If the effect does not exist within the harmony of the manifold conditions, then those manifold causes and conditions are the same as non-causes and non-conditions.
Just as milk is the causal condition for curd, if there were no curd within the milk, there would likewise be no curd in water.
If there were no curd within the milk, it would be identical to water, and one should not say that it arises solely from milk.
Therefore, the claim that there is no effect within the conjunction of various conditions is incorrect.
Question: Once the cause has performed its function as a cause for the effect and has ceased, the causal relationship still exists.
There is no such fault.
He replied:
"If the cause and the causal factor for the fruit / Having acted as the cause, then perish..."
"This cause has two natures; when one [nature] acts upon the other, it ceases.
If the cause ceases after having acted as a cause for the fruit, then that cause would possess two natures:
the first being the nature of acting as a cause.
The second [position] asserts that the cause ceases.
This is not so, because it would imply that a single dharma possesses two natures.
Therefore, the claim that the cause ceases after having acted as a cause for the effect is untenable.
Question:
If it is claimed that the cause ceases after having acted as a cause for the effect, yet the effect still arises, what fault is there?
Answer:
"If the cause does not bestow its fruit, but ceases after having acted as a cause, and the fruit arises once the cause has ceased, then that fruit would be without a cause.
If the cause does not bestow its fruit but ceases after having acted as a cause, then the fruit would arise only after the cause has already ceased; thus, that fruit would be without a cause.
This is not so. Why? Because we observe that among all effects, there is none that arises without a cause.
Therefore, your assertion that a cause ceases after having acted as a cause for its effect, yet the effect still arises, is not tenable.
Question:
What fault is there in the view that the effect arises at the very moment the various conditions conjoin?
The answer is:
"If the fruit were to arise when the various conditions have converged,
then that which arises and that which is capable of arising would exist simultaneously."
If the fruit were to arise when the various conditions conjoin, then that which arises and the act of arising would exist simultaneously.
However, this is not the case. Why is this so?
Just as a father and son cannot be born at the same time,
it is therefore not the case that a fruit arises at the moment when the various conditions combine,
as you have asserted. Question:
If the fruit were to arise first, and only later were the various conditions to come together, what fault would there be?
The answer is:
"If the fruit were to arise first, and only later were the various conditions to come together..."
"This is precisely to be separated from causes and conditions; it is called 'having no cause and effect.

If the fruit were to arise prior to the convergence of the various conditions, such a thing would not be possible; because the fruit would be separated from its causes and conditions, it would be termed "having no cause and effect."
Therefore, your claim that the fruit arises prior to the convergence of the various conditions is not tenable.
Question:
What fault is there in the view that the cause ceases and transforms into the fruit?
The answer is:
"If the cause transforms into the effect, then the cause would already have reached the effect;
in that case, the previously arisen cause would arise yet again."
There are two kinds of causes:
first, the prior-born;
second, the co-arisen.
If the cause, having ceased, were to transform into the fruit, then that previously arisen cause would have to arise once again.
But this is not the case. Why?
That which has already arisen should not arise again.
If it is claimed that this very cause transforms into the effect, that too is not so. Why?
If it were identical [to the cause], it could not be called "change"; if it were changing, it could not be called "identical.

Question: The cause does not perish entirely; rather, only its name perishes. Yet the substance of the cause transforms into the effect, just as a lump of clay transforms into a jar: the name "lump of clay" is lost, and the name "jar" arises.
Answer: When the lump of clay first ceases and the jar arises, this is not called "transformation.
Furthermore, the entity of the clay does not arise alone; jars, basins, pots, and so forth all emerge from within the clay.
If the lump of clay were merely a name, it could not transform into a jar; its transformation would be like milk transforming into curd.
Therefore, your claim that the cause transforms into the effect even though the name has ceased is incorrect.
Question:
Although the cause has ceased and perished, it is still able to produce an effect; therefore, the effect exists.
There is no such fault.
The answer is:
"How can a result arise from a cause that has perished?
Furthermore, if the cause exists within the result, how could the cause produce the result?"
If the cause has already ceased and perished, how can it produce an effect?
If the cause does not cease and yet unites with the effect, how could it produce the effect again?
Question:
If the effect already exists pervasively within the cause, how could that effect arise again?
The answer is:
"If the effect already exists pervasively within the cause, what further effect could possibly be produced?"
"Because the cause does not see the fruit, both of these do not arise.
If the cause does not see the fruit, it should not even produce the fruit, let alone see it!
If the cause does not perceive the fruit, then it should not produce the fruit.
Why is this? If it does not perceive the fruit, the fruit does not follow from the cause.
Furthermore, if the fruit does not yet exist, how can it be produced?
If the cause were already seen to possess the fruit, it should not produce it again, because the fruit would already exist. Moreover:
"If one says that there is a past cause for a past effect,
or for future and present effects, this is ultimately untenable.
If one says that there is a future cause for a future effect,"
A present cause with a past fruit is ultimately untenable.
If one says that a present cause produces a present fruit,
or a future or past fruit, this is ultimately untenable.
A past fruit does not conjoin with past, future, or present causes.
A future fruit does not conjoin with future, present, or past causes.
The present fruit does not conjoin with causes that are present, future, or past.
Likewise, these three kinds of fruits never conjoin with causes that are past, future, or present.
Furthermore:
"If there is no conjunction, how can a cause produce an effect?
If there is conjunction, how can a cause produce an effect?"
If cause and effect are not in conjunction, then there is no effect; if there is no effect, how can a cause produce an effect?
If it is claimed that a cause produces an effect at the very moment cause and effect are in conjunction, this too is not so.
Why is this? If the effect were already present within the cause, then since the effect would already exist within the cause, how could it be produced again?
Furthermore:
"If the cause is empty and lacks an effect, how can the cause produce an effect?
If the cause is not empty and possesses an effect, how can the cause produce an effect?
If the cause lacks an effect, then because it lacks an effect, the cause is empty; how then could such a cause produce an effect?

Just as a person who is not pregnant cannot give birth to a child, how could a result be produced if it already existed prior to its cause? If the result already exists because of the cause, then since it already exists, it should not be produced again.
Furthermore, we shall now explain the nature of the result.
If the fruit were not empty, it would not arise; if the fruit were not empty, it would not cease.
Because the fruit is not empty, it neither arises nor ceases.
Because the fruit is empty, it does not arise; because the fruit is empty, it does not cease.
"Because the fruit is empty, it neither arises nor ceases.
If the fruit were not empty, it should neither arise nor cease. Why is this so?

If the effect were already definitively present within the cause, it would not need to arise again; since there is no arising, there is no cessation. Therefore, because the effect is not empty, it neither arises nor ceases.
If it is claimed that because the effect is empty there is arising and ceasing, this too is not so.
Why? If the effect were empty, "empty" means non-existence; how then could there be arising and ceasing?
Therefore, it is said that because the fruit is empty, it is neither produced nor extinguished.
Furthermore, we shall now refute cause and effect by means of their identity and difference:
"If cause and effect were one, this would ultimately be impossible."
If cause and effect were different, this would also be untenable.
If cause and effect were one, that which produces and that which is produced would be identical.
If cause and effect were different, then the cause would be no different from a non-cause.
If the effect possesses a fixed intrinsic nature, how could it be produced by a cause?
If the effect lacks a fixed intrinsic nature, how could it be produced by a cause?
If the cause does not produce the effect, then the characteristic of a cause would not exist.
If there were no causal characteristics, who could possess this fruit?
If it arises from a combination of various causes and conditions,
yet that combination itself does not arise, how can it produce a fruit?
Therefore, the effect does not arise from conditions, whether they are combined or uncombined;
if there is no effect, how can there be a state of combination?
This dharma of the conjunction of various conditions cannot produce its own self-nature.
Since its own-being does not exist, how could it produce an effect?
Therefore, an effect is neither produced from the conjunction of conditions nor produced from their non-conjunction.
If there is no effect, where could there be a state of conjunction?
Chapter 21: An Examination of Formation and Destruction. Chapter Twenty-one on the Examination of Formation and Destruction, consisting of twenty verses. Question:
All worldly phenomena manifest the signs of destruction; therefore, there is destruction.
The answer is:
"Apart from formation and apart from co-formation, there is no destruction therein;
apart from destruction and apart from co-destruction, there is likewise no formation therein."
Whether there is accomplishment or no accomplishment, both are without destruction.
Whether there is destruction or no destruction, both are without accomplishment. Why is this?
"If there were no arising, how could there be ceasing?
It would be as impossible as there being death without birth.
If arising and ceasing exist simultaneously, how could there be arising and ceasing?"
Just as in the world of birth and death, neither [arising nor ceasing] occurs simultaneously.
If there is no destruction, how could there be arising?
Impermanence has never existed; it does not abide within the time of any phenomena.
If destruction were separate from formation, destruction could not be apprehended. Why?

If destruction existed apart from formation, then destruction would not depend upon formation; thus, destruction would be causeless, and furthermore, there would be no formed phenomenon that could undergo destruction.

What is called "formation" arises from the conjunction of various conditions, and what is called "disintegration" results from the dispersal of those conditions. If disintegration existed apart from formation, then in the absence of formation, who would undergo disintegration?
Just as one cannot speak of the disintegration of a jar when no jar exists, therefore, there is no disintegration apart from formation.
If it is claimed that existence and disintegration are established together, this too is not so.
Why? Because phenomena are first established individually and only subsequently undergo conjunction; yet a conjoined phenomenon does not depart from its distinctness.
If destruction were separate from disintegration, then destruction would be without cause; therefore, that which is established through conjunction would likewise not undergo destruction.

If there were establishment apart from destruction, yet no establishment occurs without the conjunction of destruction, then if establishment occurred apart from destruction, it would be permanent; and permanence is the characteristic of being indestructible.
In reality, however, no phenomenon is seen to possess a characteristic of permanence or indestructibility; therefore, there is no formation apart from destruction.
If it is claimed that formation exists simultaneously with destruction, this too is not the case.
Since formation and destruction are mutually contradictory, how could they exist at the same time?

Just as a person cannot simultaneously possess both hair and the absence of hair, so it is with formation and destruction; therefore, it is not possible for there to be formation while destruction is occurring.
Why is this? If one claims that for those who conceptually differentiate phenomena, there is always destruction within their established existence,
this is not the case.
Why is this? If arising were always accompanied by destruction, then there could be no abiding dharma; yet in reality there is abiding.
Therefore, if one is separated from destruction, or even if it coexists with destruction, there can be no arising.
Furthermore:
"Neither together nor apart can arising and ceasing be established;
since both are impossible, how could there be any establishment?"
If formation and destruction were simultaneous, there would be no formation; if they were separate, there would likewise be no formation.
If they were formed simultaneously, two mutually contradictory phenomena would exist at once—how could this be?
If they were separate, there would be no cause.
Since both gates are unestablished, how could there be establishment?
If it exists, it should be explained.
[The opponent] asks:
There currently exist phenomena characterized by exhaustion and cessation.
Regarding these phenomena characterized by exhaustion and cessation, they are described as both exhausted and not exhausted; if this were so, there would necessarily be arising and perishing.
The answer is:
"When there is exhaustion, there is no formation; when there is no exhaustion, there is also no formation.
When there is exhaustion, there is no disintegration; when there is no exhaustion, there is also no disintegration.
All phenomena are constantly extinguished moment by moment throughout day and night; the past is like flowing water that does not remain—this is what is called "exhaustion."
This matter cannot be grasped and cannot be described; it is like a mirage, for which no determinate nature can be found.
In this way, since exhaustion has no determinate nature that can be found, how could one distinguish and say that there is existence?
Therefore, the claim that there is "exhaustion" is also not established.
Since exhaustion is not established, there can likewise be no destruction; thus it is said that even exhaustion is without destruction.

Furthermore, because [dharmas] arise and perish moment by moment in constant succession without interruption, they are called "non-exhausted. Such dharmas are definitively eternally abiding and uninterrupted.
How could one distinguish and say that "now is the time of accomplishment"?
Therefore, it is said that there is neither exhaustion nor accomplishment.
Because there is no accomplishment, there is no disintegration; therefore, it is said that there is neither exhaustion nor disintegration.
Investigating in this manner, no substantial entity can be found; therefore, there is neither arising nor perishing.
Question: For now, let us set aside arising and perishing.
If there were merely "existence" as a phenomenon, what fault would there be?
The answer is:
"If one is separated from arising and ceasing, / That too is not a phenomenon."
"If one were to be separated from dharmas, there would likewise be neither arising nor ceasing.
Regarding the absence of dharmas that arise or cease: if a dharma neither arises nor ceases, that dharma must be either non-existent or eternal.
Yet in the world there is no eternal dharma; your claim that there exists a dharma apart from formation and destruction is incorrect.
Question:
If there were only formation and destruction apart from dharmas, what fault would there be?
Answer: It is also not the case that arising and ceasing exist apart from dharmas. Why is this?
If one is apart from dharmas, who could arise or perish?
Therefore, that there is arising and perishing apart from dharmas is not the case.
Furthermore:
"If the nature of phenomena is empty, who could undergo arising and ceasing?
If their nature were not empty, there likewise would be no arising or ceasing.
If the nature of all phenomena is empty, how could that which is empty undergo arising and ceasing?
If the nature of all phenomena were not empty, then being non-empty they would necessarily exist, and there could be no arising or ceasing.
Furthermore:
"If arising and ceasing were one, this would not be so."
"If formation and destruction were different, this would also not be the case.
When one investigates them, formation and destruction cannot be found as a single entity. Why is this so?
Because they possess distinct characteristics and because they involve various conceptual discriminations.
Furthermore, a difference between formation and destruction is also unattainable. Why is this?
Because there is no distinction and because there is no cause.
Furthermore:
"If one claims that arising and ceasing exist because they are seen with the eye,"
"This is merely delusion and falsehood, whereby one perceives arising and ceasing.
If it is claimed that arising and ceasing are seen with the eye, how can they be refuted through verbal expression?
This is not so. Why? Because that which perceives arising and ceasing through the eye is due to delusion and inversion.

One sees that the nature of all phenomena is empty and lacks any fixed determination, being like an illusion or a dream; it is only because of the inverted causes and conditions of past lives that ordinary beings obtain this eye, and due to the causes and conditions of recollection and conceptual discrimination in the present life, they say that the eye perceives arising and ceasing.
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is truly neither arising nor ceasing; this matter has already been explained in detail in the "Chapter on Refuting Characteristics" (*Lakṣaṇa-parivarta*).
Furthermore:
"A phenomenon does not give rise to a phenomenon, Nor does it give rise to a non-phenomenon; From a non-phenomenon, a phenomenon is not born, Nor is a non-phenomenon born from a non-phenomenon."
"From the non-dharma, neither dharma nor non-dharma arises.
Regarding the claim that dharma does not arise from dharma: whether it is lost or attained, both cases are untenable.
If a dharma arises from a dharma—whether it has already arrived or has perished—then this would be without cause. To be without cause is to fall into the extremes of nihilism or eternalism.

If a dharma arises from a dharma that has already arrived, then since that dharma is called "arising" only after it has arrived, it would be eternal; furthermore, once it has arisen, it would arise again, which would likewise be arising without cause.
This is not the case.

If that which has already perished were to give rise to a dharma, then the cause would be lost; that which arises would be without a cause. Therefore, a dharma is also not produced from what has perished.

Regarding the statement that "from dharma, non-dharma is not produced": non-dharma is defined as non-existence, while dharma is defined as existence. How could that which has characteristics (sanimitta) give rise to that which lacks characteristics (animitta)?
Therefore, from dharma, non-dharma is not produced.
Regarding the statement that "a phenomenon does not arise from what is non-dharmic": the term "non-dharmic" refers to non-existence. How can existence arise from non-existence?
If existence were to arise from non-existence, it would follow that there is no cause; to have no cause is a great error. Therefore, a phenomenon does not arise from what is non-dharmic.
That which is not produced from non-dharma is non-dharma; "non-dharma" is defined as non-existence. How could non-existence give rise to non-existence?
It is like how a rabbit's horn does not produce a tortoise's hair; therefore, non-dharma is not produced from non-dharma.
Question:
Although phenomena (*dharma*) and non-phenomena (*adharma*) are unarisen because they are distinguished in various ways, nevertheless, a phenomenon should give rise to a phenomenon. Answer:
“Phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another, nor do they arise from both self and other; how then can there be arising?
Since phenomena do not exist prior to their arising, and because that which is itself does not arise, phenomena do not arise from themselves.
If a phenomenon has not yet arisen, it likewise lacks an "other"; because there is no other, one cannot say that it arises from another.
Furthermore, if it has not yet arisen, it lacks a "self," and where there is no self, there is also no other; thus, it does not arise through both either.
If these three types do not arise, how can a phenomenon arise from a phenomenon?
Furthermore:
"If there is any phenomenon that is grasped, one immediately falls into the extremes of nihilism or eternalism."
"You should know that the phenomena one experiences— whether they be permanent or impermanent—

if one discriminates among these experienced phenomena as being wholesome or unwholesome, permanent or impermanent, and so forth, such a person will inevitably fall into either the view of eternalism or the view of nihilism."
Why is this? The dharmas that are received must be of two kinds:
either permanent or impermanent.
Neither of these two positions is tenable. Why?
Because if it were eternal, one would fall into the extreme of eternalism; if it were impermanent, one would fall into the extreme of nihilism.
Question:
"All who receive the Dharma do not fall into the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism;
because cause and effect are continuous, they are neither annihilated nor eternal."
There are those who, though they believe in and distinguish the various dharmas as they are explained, do not fall into the extremes of nihilism or eternalism.
As the sutras state, although the five aggregates are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, they are not annihilated;
and although it is said that the measure of sins and merits is not lost throughout immeasurable kalpas, they are not eternal.

Why is this? Because these dharmas, as cause and effect, constantly arise and perish in a continuous succession; thus their coming and going are unceasing. Because they arise and perish, they are not eternal; because they continue in succession, they are not annihilated.
The answer is:
"If cause and effect arise and perish, continuing in succession without interruption;
yet because what has perished does not arise again, the cause would then be subject to total annihilation."
If you say that all phenomena are neither interrupted nor eternal because they proceed in a causal succession,
yet you maintain that once a phenomenon has ceased it does not arise again, then the cause would be severed.
If it were due to cessation, how could there be continuity?
For that which has already ceased does not arise again. Furthermore:
“If phenomena abide in their own nature, there should be neither existence nor non-existence;
if nirvāṇa were the cessation of the continuum, one would fall into nihilism.

When a phenomenon is definitively present within its characteristic, at that time there is no absence of that characteristic; just as when a jar is definitively present in the form of a jar, at that time there is no characteristic of destruction.
As long as there is a jar, there is no characteristic of destruction; even when the jar is absent, there is likewise no characteristic of destruction. Why is this?
If there were no jar, there would be nothing to be destroyed; for this reason, cessation cannot be apprehended.
Because cessation is absent, there is also no arising. Why is this?
Because arising and cessation are mutually dependent conditions.
Furthermore, because there would be the faults of permanence and so forth, one should not maintain both existence and non-existence regarding a single phenomenon.

Moreover, as you previously stated that because causes and effects arise and cease in a continuous succession, one does not fall into the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism despite experiencing all phenomena.

This is not so. Why? Because you claim that since cause and effect are in continuous succession, there is a continuity of the three realms of existence (*bhava*), and that the cessation of this continuity is called *nirvāṇa*.
If that were so, at the time of nirvāṇa there would be a lapse into annihilation, because the continuity of the three realms of existence would be extinguished.
Furthermore:
"If the first existence were to cease, then there would be no subsequent existence."
"If the prior existence does not cease, there can likewise be no subsequent existence.
"Prior existence" refers to the existence of the present life; "subsequent existence" refers to the existence of future lives.
If the prior existence were to cease before the subsequent existence arises, that would be causeless.
This is not the case; therefore, one cannot say that there is a subsequent existence following the cessation of an initial existence.
If the initial existence does not cease, there likewise should be no subsequent existence.
Why is this? If the prior existence were not yet extinguished while the subsequent existence already existed, there would then be two existences at one and the same time.
This is not possible; therefore, as long as the prior existence is not extinguished, the subsequent existence does not exist.
Question:

Does future existence arise by means of the cessation of initial existence, or does it arise without cessation? Or does it arise precisely at the moment of cessation? Answer: It arises at the very moment of cessation.
"If there were a subsequent birth at the time when the initial existence ceases,
then the time of cessation would be one existence, and the time of birth would be another existence.
If there were a subsequent birth at the time when the initial existence ceases, then two existences would coexist simultaneously.
One existence is at the time of ceasing, and one existence is at the time of arising.
Question:
It is not the case that two existences can coexist at the same time—one ceasing and one arising.
"But we clearly see that when the initial existence ceases, the subsequent existence arises.
He replied:
"If one says that regarding arising and ceasing, they occur at the same time,"
"Then one dies within these very aggregates and is born within these very aggregates.

If at the time of birth and the time of death there were not two simultaneous existences, yet you claim that when the initial existence ceases, the subsequent existence arises, then one should die within whichever aggregates one currently resides and be born within those same aggregates, rather than being born within other aggregates.
Why is this? Because the one who dies is the very same as the one who is born.
Such opposing states as death and birth cannot logically exist at the same time and in the same place.

Therefore, your previous assertion that there is no simultaneous existence of both the time of cessation and the time of arising, but rather that one observes the subsequent arising at the very moment the prior existence ceases, is incorrect.
Furthermore:
"If one seeks existence within the three times, its continuity cannot be found;
if it does not exist within the three times, how could there be the continuity of existence?"
There are three kinds of existence: existence in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), existence in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Because one has not attained true wisdom within the beginningless cycle of birth and death, these three existences continue in succession eternally.
If one seeks it truthfully within the three periods of time, it cannot be found.
If it does not exist within the three periods of time, where could the continuity of existence possibly be?
One should know that the continuity of existence exists solely due to ignorance and inversion; in reality, it does not exist.

Composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna; with commentary by the Brahmin Candrakīrti.

Chapter 22: Contemplating the Tathāgata. Twenty-six verses. Question:
Among all those honored in the world, only the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is designated as the Dharma King; therefore, such an "Omniscient One" must necessarily exist.
The answer is:
Now, reflect carefully; if it exists, there is something to be grasped;
if it does not exist, what is there to be grasped?
Why is this? The Tathāgata is not the aggregates, nor is he apart from the aggregates; he does not exist within them, nor do they exist within him.
Since the Tathāgata does not possess the aggregates, where could the Tathāgata be found?
"If the Tathāgata truly exists, is the five aggregates the Tathāgata?
Does the Tathāgata exist apart from the five aggregates?
Or do the five aggregates exist within the Tathāgata?"
Is the Tathāgata within the five aggregates?
Or does the Tathāgata possess the five aggregates?
Neither of these cases is tenable.
The five aggregates are not the Tathāgata.
Why? Because they possess the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
The five aggregates possess the characteristics of arising and ceasing. If the Tathāgata were these five aggregates, then the Tathāgata would be subject to the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
If he were subject to arising and ceasing, the Tathāgata would incur faults such as impermanence and annihilationism.
Furthermore, if the recipient and the dharmas received were one and the same, then the recipient would be the Tathāgata and the dharmas received would be the five aggregates (pañca-skandha).
This is not the case; therefore, the Tathāgata is not the five aggregates.
Apart from the five aggregates, there is no Tathāgata; if there were a Tathāgata apart from the five aggregates, he would not possess the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
If that were so, the Tathāgata would incur faults such as being permanent.

Furthermore, the various faculties such as the eye cannot see or know [the Tathāgata]; however, this is not the case. Therefore, apart from the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), there is no Tathāgata, nor are the five aggregates within the Tathāgata.
Why is this? If the five aggregates were within the Tathāgata—like fruit within a vessel or a fish within water—then there would be a distinction between them.
If there were such a distinction, it would entail the aforementioned faults, such as permanence; therefore, the five aggregates do not exist within the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata does not exist within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Why?

If the Tathāgata existed within the five aggregates, it would be like a person on a bed or milk in a vessel; in such a case, there would be a distinction [between them], and the faults mentioned above would follow. Therefore, the Tathāgata does not exist within the five aggregates.
The Tathāgata likewise does not possess the five aggregates. Why is this?
If the Tathāgata possessed the five aggregates, it would be like a person having a son; in that case, there would be a distinction.
If that were so, there would be the aforementioned fault.
But this is not the case; therefore, the Tathāgata does not possess the five aggregates.
Since he cannot be found through these five modes of seeking, what then is the Tathāgata?
Question:
If, when sought according to this principle, the Tathāgata cannot be found, yet there is a Tathāgata as a combination of the five aggregates (skandhas), how is this so? Answer:
"If the Tathāgata exists through the combination of the aggregates (skandhas), then he has no self-nature (svabhāva);
if he has no self-nature, how could he exist by virtue of another?
If the Tathāgata exists because of the conjunction of the five aggregates, then he lacks self-nature.
Why is this? Because it exists due to the combination of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Question:
The Tathāgata does not exist by way of intrinsic nature, but exists only by way of extrinsic nature.
The reply is:
If there is no intrinsic nature, how can he exist by way of extrinsic nature?
Why is this? Because other-nature (parabhāva) likewise lacks intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Furthermore, because there is no cause consisting of mutual dependence, other-nature cannot be apprehended; since it cannot be apprehended, it is not designated as "other."
Furthermore:
"If a phenomenon arises dependent on another, it is therefore not-self;
if a phenomenon is not-self, how can it be the Tathāgata?"
If a phenomenon arises dependent upon various conditions, then it has no self.
Just as there is a fist because of the five fingers, yet this fist has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
so too, because of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), there is the designation "self," yet this self has no intrinsic nature.
I have various names, such as sentient being, person, deva, or Tathāgata.
If the Tathāgata exists by reason of the five aggregates, he lacks intrinsic nature; because he lacks intrinsic nature, there is no self.
If there is no self, how can one be called a Tathāgata?
Therefore, the verse says: "If a phenomenon arises dependent on another, it is therefore not-self;
if a phenomenon is not-self, how can it be the Tathāgata?"
Furthermore:
"If there is no intrinsic nature (svabhāva), how can there be extrinsic nature (parabhāva)?
Apart from intrinsic and extrinsic natures, what could be called a Tathāgata?"
If intrinsic nature does not exist, extrinsic nature (parabhāva) likewise cannot exist.

It is because of intrinsic nature that extrinsic nature is designated; since this [intrinsic nature] is absent, that [extrinsic nature] is also absent. Therefore, both intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature are non-existent.
If [the Tathāgata] is apart from self-nature and other-nature, who is the Tathāgata?
Furthermore:
"If there were a Tathāgata existing prior to the five aggregates, independent of them,"
Because one currently receives the aggregates, they are called a Tathāgata.
Now, in reality, one does not receive the aggregates; there is no further dharma of a Tathāgata.
If, by not receiving them, he is non-existent, then how could he receive them now?
If there were no appropriation, that which is appropriated could not be called "appropriated.
Since there is no such thing as a phenomenon without appropriation, it is designated as the Tathāgata.
Within the categories of identity and difference, the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended.
The fivefold search is likewise non-existent; how, then, could there be a self within the aggregates?
Furthermore, the appropriated five aggregates do not exist by way of intrinsic nature;
if they lack intrinsic nature, how could there be extrinsic nature?

If the Tathāgata existed prior to receiving the five aggregates, then that Tathāgata should have already received the five aggregates to become a Tathāgata; yet in reality, when he had not yet received the five aggregates, there was no Tathāgata beforehand—how then could he receive them now?
Furthermore, that which does not grasp the five aggregates is not called "grasping" the five aggregates; there is no such thing as one who does not grasp yet is called a Tathāgata.
Moreover, the Tathāgata cannot be found when sought among the categories of identity or difference, nor can he be found when sought in the five aggregates through the fivefold analysis.
If that were so, how could it be said that a Tathāgata exists within the five aggregates?
Furthermore, the five aggregates that are experienced do not exist by way of their own nature (svabhāva).
If it is claimed that they exist by way of another nature (parabhāva), [that too is untenable].
If it does not exist by way of its own nature,
how could it exist by way of another nature?
For what reason?
Because there is no intrinsic nature, there is also no extrinsic nature.
Furthermore:
"By this principle, sensation is empty and the feeler is empty."
"How can one use emptiness to speak of an empty Tathāgata?
Reflecting on this meaning, both sensation (*vedanā*) and the feeler (*vedaka*) are empty.
If sensation is empty, how can one use an empty sensation to speak of an empty Tathāgata?
Question: You say that both sensation (*vedanā*) and the feeler (*vedaka*) are empty; does this then imply that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) itself definitely exists?
Answer: [No.]
Not so. Why? "Emptiness cannot be spoken of; non-emptiness cannot be spoken of."
"It cannot be described as common or uncommon; it is spoken of only by means of provisional names.

One should not say that all phenomena are empty, nor should one say that all phenomena are not empty, nor should one say that all phenomena are both empty and not empty, nor should one say that they are neither empty nor not empty.
Why is this? It is merely spoken by way of conventional designation in order to refute contradictions.
When one contemplates and reflects in this manner of correct observation, one should not raise objections regarding the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Why is this? "Within the mark of quiescent extinction, there are not the four [views] such as permanence and impermanence;
within the mark of quiescent extinction, there are not the four [views] such as finitude and infinitude."
The true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus subtle, wondrous, and quiescent; yet, due to the past, four kinds of false views arise:
that the world is eternal, that the world is non-eternal, that the world is both eternal and non-eternal, and that the world is neither eternal nor non-eternal.
Within this state of quiescence, none of these exist at all.
Why is this? Because the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is ultimately pure and cannot be grasped; even emptiness is not accepted, let alone the four kinds of views.
These four kinds of views are all produced by grasping (*upādāna*), whereas the true reality of all phenomena has no cause for grasping.
All four types of views regard one's own view as noble and others' views as base; yet in the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there is neither "this" nor "that.
Therefore, it is said that within cessation (*śānti*), the four types of views do not exist.
Just as there are four kinds of views based on the past life, so too are there four kinds of views based on the future life:
that the world is finite, that the world is infinite, that the world is both finite and infinite, and that the world is neither finite nor infinite.
Question:
If the Tathāgata is analyzed in this manner, does it mean that there is no Tathāgata? Answer:
"Those whose false views are deep and heavy say that there is no Tathāgata;
yet the Tathāgata’s mark of quiescent extinction cannot be conceptualized as existing either.
There are two kinds of false views:
First, it destroys worldly happiness;
second, it destroys the path to nirvana.
That which destroys worldly happiness is a coarse and false view, asserting that there is neither sin nor merit, and that there are no Tathāgatas or other noble sages.
To give rise to such false views and abandon the good for the evil is to destroy worldly happiness.
To destroy the path to Nirvana is to be greedily attached to a self, to discriminate between existence and non-existence, and to conceive of generating good and extinguishing evil.
Because one gives rise to wholesome states, one attains worldly happiness; because one discriminates between existence and non-existence, one does not attain nirvana.
Therefore, if one says that the Tathāgata does not exist, this is a profound and deep-seated false view; it results in the loss of even worldly happiness, let alone nirvana!
If one says that there is a Tathāgata, this too is a false view.
Why? Because the Tathāgata is characterized by quiescence, yet one discriminates him in various ways.
Therefore, within the state of quiescent extinction, it is also incorrect to differentiate that a Tathāgata exists.
"Thus, within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, even contemplation is impossible;
regarding whether a Tathāgata exists or does not exist after parinirvāṇa, one should not engage in such differentiation."
Because the true nature of all dharmas is emptiness, one should not contemplate whether the Tathāgata exists, does not exist, or both exists and does not exist after his parinirvāṇa.
Since the Tathāgata has been ultimately empty from the very beginning, how much more so after his passing!
“The Tathāgata has transcended conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), yet people give rise to conceptual proliferation;
conceptual proliferation destroys the eye of wisdom, and thus they all fail to see the Buddha.
Conceptual proliferation refers to recollecting, grasping at signs, and discriminating between "this" and "that."

To speak of whether the Buddha perishes or does not perish and so forth is mere frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*); because it obscures the eye of wisdom, one cannot see the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
Within this "Chapter on the Tathāgata," through contemplation from beginning to middle to end, the fixed nature of the Tathāgata is found to be unattainable.
Therefore, the verse says:
“The nature possessed by the Tathāgata Is precisely the nature of the world;
The Tathāgata has no nature, And the world likewise has no nature.”
In this chapter, through contemplation and investigation, it is shown that the *tathāgatagarbha* is the very nature of all the world.
Question: What is the *tathāgatagarbha*?
Answer: The Tathāgata has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); he is the same as the world in being without intrinsic nature.
Chapter 23: Examination of Perversions (*viparyāsa*). Verse 24. Question:
"From conceptualization and discrimination, greed, hatred, and delusion arise;
the inversions of purity and impurity all arise from a multitude of conditions.
The Sūtra states that based on the inversions of purity and impurity, conceptualization and discrimination give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion.
Therefore, one should know that greed, anger, and delusion exist.
He replied:
"If, due to the pure and the impure, the three poisons arise from perversion,"
"The three poisons are devoid of intrinsic nature; therefore, afflictions have no reality.
If all afflictions arise from pure and impure inverted conceptualizations and discriminations, they lack self-nature; for this reason, all afflictions have no reality.
Furthermore:
"Whether the self exists or does not exist, this matter is ultimately unestablished;
likewise, whether the various afflictions exist or do not exist, they too are unestablished."

"I have no causal conditions by which 'existence' or 'non-existence' could be established; now that the self and all afflictions do not exist, how could they be established as either existent or non-existent? Why is this so?"
"Whoever possesses these afflictions is, by that very fact, not established;
if they existed apart from this [person], then the afflictions would have no owner.
Afflictions are so called because they afflict others; those who afflict others must be sentient beings, yet such sentient beings cannot be found when sought everywhere.
If one claims that afflictions exist apart from sentient beings, then those afflictions would have no locus to which they belong.
If one claims that although there is no self, afflictions nevertheless belong to the mind, this too is not the case.
Why is this? "Just as the fivefold view of a self cannot be found when sought,
so too afflictions within the defiled mind cannot be found through the fivefold search."
"Just as the view of a self cannot be found through five modes of seeking within the five aggregates,
so too all afflictions cannot be found through five modes of seeking within the defiled mind."
Furthermore, within the afflictions, a defiled mind cannot be found even when sought in five ways.
Moreover:
"Purity and impurity are inversions; these lack intrinsic nature."
"How is it that from these two, all afflictions arise?
Regarding the inversion of purity and impurity: "inversion" means falsehood.
If it is false, it lacks intrinsic nature; if it lacks intrinsic nature, there is no inversion.
If there were no inversion, how could the various afflictions arise because of inversion?
It is asked:
"Form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects constitute the six kinds."
"These six kinds are the root of the three poisons.

These six sense bases are the root of the three poisons; from these six sense bases arise the inversions of purity and impurity, and from the inversions of purity and impurity arise greed, hatred, and delusion.
The answer is:
"Form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and the sixfold nature of phenomena—
all are empty like a mirage or a dream, like a city of the gandharvas."
Within these six kinds, what purity or impurity can there be?
They are like conjured illusions and like reflections in a mirror.

The intrinsic nature of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects, when not yet in conjunction with the mind, is empty and non-existent; they are like a mirage, like a dream, like a conjuration, and like a reflection in a mirror—merely deceiving and deluding the mind, without any fixed characteristics.
Thus, within these six sense bases, what purity or impurity could there be?
Furthermore:
"Without depending on the characteristic of purity, there is no such thing as impurity."
Because purity gives rise to impurity, there is therefore no such thing as impurity.
If it were not due to purity, impurity would not have existed previously; by what cause, then, could one speak of impurity?
Therefore, there is no impurity.
Furthermore:
"Because there is no impurity, there is likewise no purity."
"Because of impurity there is purity; therefore, there is no such thing as purity.
If purity did not previously exist independent of impurity, on what basis could one speak of purity?
Therefore, there is no purity.
Furthermore:
"If there is no purity, by what means could desire arise?"
"If there were no impurity, by what means could there be anger?
Since there is neither purity nor impurity, greed and anger do not arise.
Question:
The Sūtras speak of four inversions, such as the inversion of permanence and so forth.
If one perceives permanence within the impermanent, this is called an inversion;
if one perceives impermanence within the impermanent, this is not an inversion.
The other three inversions are also like this.
Since inversion exists, the one who possesses inversion must also exist; why then do you say that none exist at all?
The answer is:
"To cling to permanence within the impermanent is called a perversion;
since there is no permanence within emptiness, where could there be the perversion of permanence?
If one clings to permanence within that which is impermanent, it is termed a perversion.
In the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, there is no permanence; how, then, could there be the inversion of permanence therein?
The same applies to the other three [inversions].
Furthermore:
"If, within impermanence, one clings to impermanence, this is not an inversion;
yet in emptiness there is no impermanence—how could there be non-inversion?

If clinging to impermanence while saying "this is impermanent" were not called an inversion, then since there is no impermanence within the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena, and because impermanence does not exist, who would be in a state of non-inversion?
The other three [stanzas] are also like this.
Furthermore:
"The one who clings, the act of clinging, And the phenomena to which one clings— all these are empty."
"All these are marks of quiescent extinction; how could there be attachment?

That which is called "name" refers to things; that which is called "attachment" refers to the agent; that which is called "name" refers to karma; and that which is called "the means employed" refers to the activity performed—all of these are empty of intrinsic nature and are marks of quiescent extinction.
As stated in the "Tathāgata Chapter," there is therefore no attachment.
Furthermore:
"If there were no dharma of attachment, to call it 'false' would be a perversion."
To say that "correct" means not being inverted— who could possibly possess such a thing?
To be attached to names, recollections, conceptualizations, and distinctions such as "this" and "that," or "existence" and "non-existence"—
if one were free from such attachment, who would be subject to error and inversion?
Who is it that is correct and not inverted?
Furthermore:
"The inverted does not give rise to inversion; The non-inverted does not give rise to inversion."
The mistaken does not give rise to the mistaken, nor does the non-mistaken give rise to it.
Even at the time of being mistaken, the mistaken does not arise;
you should examine for yourself: who gives rise to the mistaken?
"Those who have already fallen into perversion do not further give rise to perversion, because they have already fallen into it.
Those who are not subject to perversion are likewise not subject to perversion, because in them there is no perversion."
Even at the time of inversion, there is no inversion, for that would entail two faults.
Now, setting aside your prideful mind, observe carefully for yourself: who is it that undergoes inversion?
Furthermore:
"If no inversions arise, how can this principle exist?
Since there are no inversions, who could be one who possesses inversions?"
Because the various causes and conditions of perversion have been destroyed, one falls into non-arising.
One becomes attached to this non-arising, claiming that non-arising is the true reality of perversion.
Therefore, the verse says: How can that which is called "non-arising" be termed an inversion?
Since even untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas are not even designated as having the characteristic of non-arising, how much less could an inversion have the characteristic of non-arising?
Since inversion does not exist, how can there be one who possesses inversion?
It is because of inversion that there is one who possesses inversion.
Furthermore:
"If permanence, self, bliss, and purity were truly existent, then this permanence, self, bliss,
and purity would not be a perversion. If permanence, self, bliss,
and purity possessed these four as truly existent natures, then this permanence, self, bliss, and purity would not be a perversion.
Why is this? Because there must be a real entity.
How, then, can it be called an inversion?

If it is argued that the perversions of permanence, self, pleasure, and purity do not exist because their opposites—impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity—are the four [noble truths] that must truly exist and thus cannot be called perversions; [then this argument is flawed].
It is called "non-inverted" because it is the opposite of inversion;
however, this is not the case. Why?
"If permanence, self, bliss, and purity do not exist in reality;
then impermanence, suffering, and impurity should likewise not exist.
If these four—permanence, self, bliss, and purity—are non-existent in reality, then because they are absent, the four factors such as impermanence and so forth should also not exist.
Why is this? Because there is no mutual dependence among signless phenomena.
Furthermore:
"When such inversion ceases, ignorance likewise ceases;
because ignorance has ceased, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth also cease.
"Such" means according to its meaning.

Because all inversions are extinguished, the fundamental ignorance of the twelve links of dependent origination is also extinguished; because ignorance is extinguished, the three types of karmic formations up to old age and death are all extinguished.
Furthermore:
"If the nature of the afflictions were real and possessed of a locus,
how could they ever be severed?"
“Who can sever its nature?
If these afflictions were themselves inverted and possessed a real intrinsic nature, how could they be severed?
Who could sever that nature?
If it is claimed that all afflictions are false and devoid of intrinsic nature, and thus can be severed, this is also not the case. Why?
"If afflictions were false, devoid of intrinsic nature and without a basis,..."
"How can they be severed?
Who is able to sever that which lacks intrinsic nature?
If all afflictions are false and devoid of intrinsic nature, then they belong to nothing; how, then, can they be severed?
Who can sever the dharmas that lack intrinsic nature?
Chapter Twenty-Four: Contemplation of the Four Noble Truths. Within this chapter, consisting of forty verses, it is asked:
By destroying the four inversions and penetrating the four noble truths, one attains the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
"If all things were empty, there would be neither arising nor ceasing;
in that case, the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths would not exist.
Because the Four Truths would be absent, there would be no seeing of suffering or abandoning of its origin."
The realization of cessation and the cultivation of the path—such things as these do not exist.
Because these things do not exist, there are no fruits of the four paths;
because the four fruits do not exist, those who are attaining them likewise do not exist.
If the eight noble persons did not exist, there would be no Jewel of the Sangha;
because the Four Truths do not exist, there would likewise be no Jewel of the Dharma;
and because the Jewels of the Dharma and Sangha do not exist, there would also be no Jewel of the Buddha.
"To speak of emptiness in such a manner is to destroy the Triple Gem.
If all that exists in the world were empty and non-existent, then there would be neither arising nor ceasing.
Because there is neither arising nor ceasing, there would be no Four Noble Truths.
Why is this? From the Truth of Origination arises the Truth of Suffering; the Truth of Origination is the cause, and the Truth of Suffering is the effect.
The cessation of the truth of the origin of suffering is called the truth of cessation; that which leads to the truth of cessation is called the truth of the path.
The truth of the path is the cause, and the truth of cessation is the fruit.
Thus, these four truths possess both cause and fruit; if there were neither arising nor cessation, then the four truths would not exist.
Because the Four Truths do not exist, there is no seeing of suffering, abandoning of the origin, realizing of cessation, or cultivating the path.
Because seeing suffering, abandoning the origin, realizing cessation, and cultivating the path do not exist, there are no four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Because the four fruits of śrāmaṇya do not exist, there are no practitioners of the four paths nor those who have attained the four fruits.
If these eight noble ones do not exist, then the Jewel of the Saṃgha does not exist.
Furthermore, because the Four Noble Truths do not exist, the Jewel of the Dharma also does not exist.
If there were no Dharma Jewel and no Sangha Jewel, how could there be a Buddha?
One who attains the Dharma is called a Buddha; if there is no Dharma, how can there be a Buddha?
You claim that all phenomena are empty, and thus you destroy the Three Jewels.
Furthermore:
"The dharma of emptiness destroys cause and effect, and it also destroys both sin and merit;
it moreover utterly ruins all worldly dharmas."
"If one were to accept that all phenomena are empty, then one would negate both demerit and merit, as well as the karmic retribution of demerit and merit;
one would also negate conventional reality. Because there are such faults as these, all phenomena ought not to be empty."
The answer was:
"You truly cannot now understand the causes and conditions of emptiness within emptiness, nor do you know the meaning of emptiness;
for this reason, you give rise to distress within yourself."
"You do not understand what the characteristic of emptiness is,
nor for what causes and conditions emptiness is taught;
furthermore, you do not understand the meaning of emptiness."
Because they cannot know things as they truly are, such doubts and difficulties arise.
Furthermore:
"The Buddhas rely on the two truths / To teach the Dharma to sentient beings."
First is the conventional truth, and second is the ultimate truth.
If a person cannot understand these two truths through their differentiation,
they will not know the true meaning within the profound Buddha-dharma.

Regarding conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*): although the nature of all phenomena is empty, because worldly beings are subject to inversion, they give rise to false phenomena which are considered real within the world.

Because the noble sages truly know the nature of inversion, they know that all phenomena are empty and unarisen; for these noble ones, this is the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), which is called "real."
The Buddhas rely upon these two truths to teach the Dharma to sentient beings.
If a person cannot correctly discern the two truths as they truly are, they will not understand the true meaning of the profound Buddha-dharma.

If it is claimed that because all phenomena are non-arising, the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) alone suffices and a second conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) is unnecessary, this is also not the case. Why is this so?
"If one does not rely on conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), one cannot attain the ultimate truth (paramārtha);
if one does not attain the ultimate truth, then one cannot attain nirvāṇa.
Since the ultimate truth is entirely dependent upon verbal expression, and verbal expression is conventional, if one does not rely on the conventional, the ultimate truth cannot be expressed.
If the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) were not attained, how could one reach nirvāṇa?
Therefore, although all phenomena are without arising, there are two truths.
Furthermore:
"If one cannot correctly contemplate emptiness, the dull-witted will bring harm upon themselves,
like one unskilled in incantations or one who improperly grasps a venomous snake.
If a person of dull faculties does not properly understand the dharma of emptiness, they will err regarding emptiness and give rise to false views.
It is like grasping a venomous snake for the sake of profit; if one cannot grasp it skillfully, one will instead be harmed by it.
It is also like a spell or incantation; if one wishes to accomplish something but cannot do so skillfully, it will instead turn back and harm oneself.
The same applies to those of dull faculties who contemplate the dharma of emptiness.
Furthermore:
"The World-Honored One knows this dharma, its profoundly deep and subtle characteristics."
"It is not within the reach of those with dull faculties; therefore, I do not wish to speak.
Because the Dharma is exceedingly profound and subtle, it is not understood by those with dull faculties; for this reason, the World-Honored One does not wish to speak.
Furthermore:
"You claim that I am attached to emptiness, and thus you impute a fault to me;
yet the fault you have now imputed does not exist within emptiness."
"You claim that because I am attached to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), you find fault with me.
However, regarding the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) which I teach, that emptiness is itself empty; thus, such a fault does not exist.
Furthermore:"
"Because the principle of emptiness exists, all phenomena are established;
if the principle of emptiness did not exist, nothing at all would be established.
Because the principle of emptiness exists, all mundane and supramundane phenomena are fully accomplished.
If the meaning of emptiness did not exist, then nothing at all would be established.
Furthermore:
"You now have faults of your own, yet you turn them back upon me."

"Just as a person riding a horse might forget the very horse he is riding upon, so too you fail to perceive your own faults within the realm of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), yet you perceive faults in emptiness (*śūnyatā*). You are like that person who, while mounted on a horse, has forgotten the horse he rides."
Why is this? "If you perceive all phenomena as having a determinate intrinsic nature,
then you perceive all phenomena as being without cause and without condition."
"You assert that all phenomena possess a fixed nature.
If that were so, one would perceive all phenomena as being without cause and without condition. Why is this?"
If phenomena possessed a determinate intrinsic nature, they would be neither produced nor extinguished; what need, then, would there be for causes and conditions?
If all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, then they possess no intrinsic nature.
Therefore, if all phenomena were to possess a fixed intrinsic nature, they would lack causes and conditions.
If one claims that all phenomena definitely abide in their own intrinsic nature, this is not so. Why is that?
"This would destroy cause and effect, as well as the agent, the action, and the instrument;
it would likewise ruin the arising and ceasing of all things.
If phenomena possessed a fixed nature, then such matters as cause and effect would not exist.
As the verse says:
"Phenomena born of various causes and conditions, I say they are 'non-existent,' yet they are also provisional names, and this is the meaning of the Middle Way."
"There has never been a single dharma that does not arise from causes and conditions;
therefore, there is no dharma whatsoever that is not empty.
"Dharmas produced by various causes and conditions—I say they are themselves emptiness."

Why is this? Because things arise through the complete assembly and conjunction of various conditions; since these things depend upon those various causes and conditions, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty; and emptiness itself is also empty.

It is merely for the sake of guiding sentient beings that it is spoken of by means of provisional names; because it is free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence, it is called the Middle Way.
Since this dharma lacks intrinsic nature, it cannot be said to exist; yet, because there is no emptiness [to be found], it cannot be said to be non-existent.

If a phenomenon possessed an intrinsic nature or characteristic, it would exist without depending on various conditions; yet if it does not depend on various conditions, it cannot exist as a phenomenon. Therefore, there is no phenomenon that is not empty.
As for the fault you attributed to the teaching of emptiness above, that fault now returns to you.
Why is this? "If all things were not empty, there would be neither arising nor ceasing."
"In this way, the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths would not exist.
If all phenomena each possessed their own intrinsic nature and were not empty, then there would be no arising or ceasing.
Because there is no arising or ceasing, the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths would not exist. Why is this?
"If suffering does not arise from conditions, how could suffering exist?"
Impermanence is the meaning of suffering; that which has a fixed nature cannot be impermanent.
Since suffering does not arise from conditions, there is no suffering. Why is this?
The Sūtras state that impermanence is the meaning of suffering.
If suffering possessed a fixed nature, how could it be impermanent?
For it would not relinquish its own intrinsic nature.
Furthermore:
"If suffering possessed an intrinsic nature, why would it arise from origination?
Therefore, there is no origination, because that would destroy the meaning of emptiness."
If suffering possessed a fixed nature, it could not arise again, as it would already exist.
If that were the case, there would be no Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), because the meaning of emptiness would be undermined by its destruction.
Furthermore:
"If suffering possessed an intrinsic nature, it could not undergo cessation.
Because you cling to an intrinsic nature, you thereby subvert the Truth of Cessation."
If suffering possessed an intrinsic nature, it could not be extinguished.
Why? Because that which possesses an intrinsic nature is indestructible.
Furthermore:
"If suffering possessed a fixed nature, there would be no cultivation of the path;
if the path can be cultivated, it possesses no fixed nature."
If dharmas were definitively existent, then there would be no cultivation of the path. Why is this?
If a dharma is real, it is eternal; and that which is eternal cannot be increased.
If the Path were something to be cultivated, then the Path would lack a fixed nature.
Furthermore:
"If there were no Truth of Suffering, nor the Truths of Origination and Cessation..."
"What is the path by which suffering is extinguished, and where does it ultimately lead?
If all phenomena were inherently existent from the outset, then the truths of suffering, its origin, and its cessation would not exist.
Now, regarding the path that extinguishes suffering, where exactly does it lead to the state of the extinction of suffering?
Furthermore:
"If suffering possessed a fixed intrinsic nature, it would not have been perceived from the outset."
"How can it be seen now?
For its nature does not differ.
If one could not see the nature of suffering when previously an ordinary person, then one should likewise be unable to see it now.
Why is this? Because the nature [of things] is not seen as fixed.
Furthermore:
"Just as seeing suffering is not so, so too the abandoning of the origin, the realization of cessation,
the cultivation of the path, and the four fruits— all these are likewise not so.
Just as with the nature of the Truth of Suffering, that which was not previously seen should not be seen later either.
In this way, there should likewise be no abandoning of the origin, realization of cessation, or cultivation of the path. Why is this?
Because the nature of this origin has not been severed from the beginning, it should not be severed now either, for its nature is indestructible.
Cessation was not realized previously; it should not be realized now either, because it was not realized previously.
The Path was not cultivated previously; it should not be cultivated now either, because it was not cultivated previously.
Therefore, the four types of practice—seeing, abandoning, realizing, and cultivating—the Four Noble Truths, should not exist.
Since these four types of practice do not exist, the four paths and their fruits likewise do not exist.
Why is this? "The nature of these four fruits of the path was unobtainable from the beginning;
if the nature of all phenomena were fixed, how could it be obtained now?"
"If all phenomena possessed a fixed nature, how could the four fruits of śrāmaṇya—which were previously unattained—be attained now?
If they can be attained, then their nature is not fixed."
Furthermore:
"If the four fruits did not exist, there would be no one attaining them or progressing toward them;
because the eight noble ones would not exist, the Jewel of the Saṅgha would not exist."
Because there would be no four fruits of śrāmaṇya, there would be no one who has attained the fruits nor anyone progressing toward them.
Because there would be no eight noble persons (āryapudgala), there would be no Saṃgha Jewel;
yet the Sūtras state that the eight noble persons are called the Saṃgha Jewel.
Furthermore:
"Because the Four Noble Truths do not exist, there is likewise no Jewel of the Dharma;
without the Jewel of the Dharma, there is no Jewel of the Saṃgha—how, then, could there be the Jewel of the Buddha?"

One attains the dharma of nirvāṇa by practicing the Four Noble Truths; if there were no Four Truths, there would be no Dharma Jewel. If these two jewels did not exist, how could there be a Buddha Jewel?
By asserting that all phenomena possess such an intrinsic nature based on these reasons, you destroy the Three Jewels.
[The opponent] asks:
Although you refute all phenomena, the ultimate path of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* must exist; it is because of this path that one is called a Buddha.
The answer is:
"According to your statement, there is no Buddha by reason of bodhi;
nor is there bodhi by reason of a Buddha."

"If you maintain that all phenomena possess a fixed nature, then it would be impossible for a Buddha to exist because of bodhi, or for bodhi to exist because of a Buddha, since the natures of these two would be eternally fixed."
Furthermore: "Though one may exert diligent effort and practice the path to enlightenment,
if one does not originally possess the Buddha-nature, one should not be able to attain Buddhahood."
Because they lack an inherent nature from the outset, it is like iron that lacks the nature of gold; even though it is repeatedly forged and refined, it will never become gold.
Furthermore:
"If all phenomena were not empty, there would be no performing of sins or merits."
"What would non-emptiness do?
Because its nature is fixed.
If all phenomena were not empty, there would ultimately be no one who could commit sins or cultivate merit.
Why is this? Because the nature of demerit and merit has already been predetermined, and furthermore, because there is neither action nor an agent. Moreover:
"If you hold that within demerit and merit there is no production of retribution,
